muscles.name: Protractor pectoralis / cucullaris
muscles.developmental: Branchiomeric. Derives from cranial paraxial/lateral plate mesoderm caudal to the last pharyngeal arch, not from somites — the defining muscle of the head–trunk boundary.

consensus.origin: Fascia over the occiput and anterior epaxial/axial musculature; in gnathostome fishes, the dorsal edge of the branchial region.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal margin of the pectoral girdle — scapula, suprascapula, or cleithrum.
consensus.action: Protracts and stabilises the pectoral girdle against the head and axial skeleton; in mammals, elevates and rotates the scapula.
consensus.innervation: Accessory nerve (CN XI) or its non-mammalian equivalent — caudal branchial branches of the vagus complex. Not spinal.

occurrences.name: Cucullaris
occurrences.action: Elevates the branchial arches and stabilises the girdle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias. The information was in this row's own `origin`/`insertion` prose and had never been structured; Ziermann et al. also resolve the insertion further than the prose did, naming the scapular process, the posterior epibranchial cartilages and the anterior extrabranchial cartilages as three separate ends. No origin row: the sheet arises from the fascia beside the epaxial musculature and touches no element there, which is why a muscle that spans the head-trunk boundary leaves nothing for a fossil to record at its front end. The same dissection failed to find the 'levatores arcuum branchialium' of Kesteven (1942) in either Squalus or Mustelus laevis, so the levator half of this record's Chondrichthyes name is on Kesteven's authority and not on theirs.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis
occurrences.note: Lepisosteus osseus. The cucullaris develops from the same cranial mesoderm population as the branchial constrictors, supporting a branchiomeric rather than somitic origin. Naumann et al. also report that the muscle has been misidentified in earlier work on this fish.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis (cucullaris)
occurrences.action: Draws the girdle anterodorsally.
occurrences.innervation: Accessory nerve equivalent; developmentally distinct from the levator scapulae, which is somitic.
occurrences.note: Sefton et al. (2016) show the cucullaris and the somitic levator scapulae are separable by developmental origin even where they are topographically adjacent — the strongest available test of this homology.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Two heads arising together and diverging posteriorly. The anterior head lands between the procoracohumeralis and the dorsalis scapulae, which is the topological fix on its identity.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia and the posterior surface of the skull.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior head onto the lateral surfaces of the procoracoid and scapula; posterior head onto the anterolateral border of the scapula.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus. Origin: Occipital region and cervical fascia. Insertion: Anterior margin of the scapula and suprascapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis (episternocleidomastoideus, partim)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. Meers's m. trapezius, this record's crocodylian occurrence. A thin sheet from the thoracodorsal fascia ventrolateral to the median row of dorsal scutes, inserting fleshily in Crocodylus acutus and by an aponeurotic sheet in other species along the cranial edge of the scapula dorsal to the acromion. Its origin can look continuous with that of latissimus dorsi but is always separable. **No acromion row, and that is now a decision rather than a workaround.** The acromion is scored present in Crocodylia (see skeleton.json), but Meers places this insertion *dorsal to* it, on the cranial edge of the scapula — the acromion is his reference point, not the attachment site. Two other crocodylian muscles in this dataset do attach to it.
occurrences.divisionNote: No division recorded. '(episternocleidomastoideus, partim)' says the crocodylian muscle corresponds *in part* to the mammalian one, which is a hedge about homology and not a subdivision of this muscle in the alligator.

occurrences.name: Cucullaris capitis / cucullaris cervicis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus. Insertion: Clavicle and scapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Trapezius (+ sternocleidomastoideus)
occurrences.action: Elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.
occurrences.innervation: Accessory nerve (CN XI), with a proprioceptive contribution from the cervical ventral rami.
occurrences.note: The mammalian trapezius and sternocleidomastoid are subdivisions of a single cucullaris field. Their retention of CN XI innervation, despite lying entirely within the neck and trunk, is the classic evidence that innervation tracks developmental origin rather than topographic position.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Trapezius, both bellies. Pars cervicalis from the cervical raphe between C3-4 and T1, pars thoracica from the thoracic raphe between T2 and T8, inserting on the distal two-thirds of the cranial margin of the scapular spine and often reaching the metacromion. Every origin is raphe or fascia, not bone — which is why a muscle this large leaves so little for a fossil to record.

occurrences.name: Trapezius
occurrences.action: Rotates the scapular blade, probably assisting protraction of the forelimb.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Reconstructed with no osteological correlate of its own** — the trapezius follows the levator scapulae here, and only that. Neither muscle is present in birds, so both rest on a single argument: if they were lost with the reorientation of the scapular blade into the avian subhorizontal position, they can be restored in theropods that never had that orientation. The levator scapulae at least has a scar in ceratosaurs, tetanurans and tyrannosaurids to bracket back from; the trapezius has nothing, and is reconstructed because the levator scapulae was. Origin from the median cervical and thoracodorsal fascia as in crocodylians and lepidosaurs (Meers 2003; Russell & Bauer 2008). The insertion is scored on the acromion because in crocodylians it intermingles with the levator scapulae insertion; Burch restricts the trapezius to the proximal part of that shared site.

occurrences.name: Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid
occurrences.action: Trapezius elevates, depresses, retracts and superiorly rotates the scapula; sternocleidomastoid flexes and rotates the head.
occurrences.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (XI), with proprioceptive fibres from C3-C4.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The clearest single row for what this record is**: the human cucullaris has split in two and the two halves look nothing alike, but both are still innervated by the spinal accessory nerve, which is the criterion the whole homology rests on. The trapezius keeps the ancestral head-to-girdle course; the sternocleidomastoid has reversed it, taking a new origin on the sternum and clavicle and inserting on the skull, so that a girdle protractor became a head rotator without changing its nerve. Gest gives the trapezius insertion as the lateral third of the clavicle, the medial acromion and the crest and tubercle of the scapular spine — three named sites on what is one continuous line in a lizard. The sternocleidomastoid insertion is scored on the occiput because the mastoid process is not a separate element here.

occurrences.name: M. episternocleidomastoideus and M. trapezius
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Russell & Bauer reverse the usual reading of which end is which, and the reason is this record's own logic.** The episternocleidomastoideus is normally described as inserting on the skull; they argue that taken with its developmental associate the trapezius, the cranial attachment is a functional insertion but an anatomical origin, and the girdle attachment the true insertion — which is how the cucullaris is described for fishes. So the rows here run skull to girdle. Origin from the ascending process of the parietal and the posterolateral paroccipital process of the exoccipital, and from the neural spines of the third cervical to the fourth dorsal vertebra; insertion onto the lateral process of the interclavicle and the sternum, and onto the acromion and the anterodorsal clavicle. Fürbringer (1900) recognised the two as one unit in lizards, and they run from an undivided cucullaris-like sheet in *Gekko* and *Lacerta* to complete separation in *Phrynosoma*.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). From the thoracodorsal fascia along the vertebral spinous processes in the midline — fascia, so the row carries the vertebral column and not a named vertebral group, because Freitas et al. do not say which vertebrae. It runs to the cranial margin of the scapula, some of its fibres intermingling with the dorsal margin of the deltoideus scapularis and passing over it, which Freitas et al. also report for *Alligator mississippiensis*. **They match the muscle to the crocodilian condition and explicitly against the lizard one**: the two-bellied *V. exanthematicus* trapezius of Jenkins & Goslow (1983), with its cranial belly from the supraspinal ligament and nuchal fascia and its caudal belly from a separate aponeurosis, is said to be quite unlike what they found. Russell & Bauer put this animal's trapezius on this record too, but as one unit with the episternocleidomastoideus and running the other way — skull to girdle — so the two readings differ over which end is the insertion as well as over the attachments.

occurrences.name: M. capiti-dorso-clavicularis (cucullaris)
occurrences.innervation: N. accessorius, with cervical nerves IV, V and VI.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Osawa's muscle 1, and he names it *cucullaris* outright. A very broad sheet from the parietal, squamosal and supraoccipital, from the cervical fascia and from the spinous processes of the eleven anterior vertebrae, inserting along the upper border of the clavicle. **In one specimen he could split it**: a small cleft near the insertion separated a capiti-dorso-clavicularis from an episterno-cleido-mastoideus, which is this record's division in a taxon that usually shows it undivided. The innervation is the criterion the record rests on — accessorius plus cervical IV-VI, exactly as in the human trapezius and sternocleidomastoid scored here from Gest.

occurrences.name: Trapezius and cleido-mastoid
occurrences.divisionNote: The cleido-occipital, present in the cuscus and the phascogale, is absent in the thylacine — Cunningham states it directly.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The trapezius has the same origin in all three of Cunningham's marsupials — occipital crest, every cervical spine, and the spines of the seven anterior thoracic vertebrae — and the same posterior insertion into the scapular spine and the root of the acromion. What differs is the anterior, humeral division, and in the thylacine it is the most strongly marked of the three: it sweeps over the head of the humerus, some of its deeper fibres mixing with the other muscles gathered on the vestigial clavicle, and **ends entirely in the clavicular deltoid** rather than on bone. **The cleido-occipital is absent in this animal** and present in the other two, so its part row is missing here rather than scored no. The cleido-mastoid runs the other way from its neighbours': it holds the mastoid region in front and travels back as a narrow fleshy band, half inserting into the inner end of the vestigial clavicle and half continuing into the clavicular deltoid. The lateral occipital row is that mastoid attachment.

occurrences.name: Trapezius group
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Origin and scapular insertion as in the other two. Of the anterior fibres that pass over the humeral head, a very few — those making the muscle's free anterior margin — reach the clavicle; the rest fuse with **both** the acromial and the clavicular deltoid, which is what makes this animal's cephalo-humeral muscle a three-part composite where the thylacine's and the phascogale's are two-part. The cleido-occipital is a narrow slip lying so closely on the cleido-mastoid that it is not apparent at first: clavicle (sternal end) behind, occipital ridge in front, on the same plane as the trapezius and the sterno-mastoid. The cleido-mastoid runs from the same end of the clavicle to the mastoid region under cover of the sterno-mastoid.

occurrences.name: Trapezius group
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. As in the cuscus, with one difference Cunningham singles out: **none of the anterior trapezius fibres join the acromial deltoid — all enter the clavicular portion.** The cleido-occipital is better marked here than in the cuscus, cleanly separable from the cleido-mastoid along its whole length, and it fuses with the anterior margin of the trapezius as it nears the occiput. Cunningham notes that Macalister records no cleido-occipital in either the wombat or the Tasmanian devil, and that Cuvier & Laurillard figure one in the opossum and in *Macropus minor* but not in *Phalangista cavifrons* — so its presence here is a real character, not a default.

occurrences.name: Trapezius and cleidomastoid series
occurrences.divisionNote: Six here against a human's two. The dorsocutaneous is the one Diogo et al. record in the platypus and in none of the other eight taxa in their table.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 3. **This record's identity stated by a source that puts it in the branchial chapter, not the pectoral one.** They list the mammalian acromiotrapezius, spinotrapezius, dorsocutaneous, cleido-occipitalis, sternocleidomastoideus, cleidomastoideus and sternomastoideus as corresponding to the reptilian trapezius and sternocleidomastoideus, and those in turn to the protractor pectoralis of amphibians, dipnoans and other osteichthyans — which is exactly this record. They add the reason it is filed apart from the true branchial muscles: **the protractor pectoralis is not a branchial muscle *sensu stricto* because it moves the pectoral girdle and not the branchial arches.** A muscle sorted by what it does rather than where it came from, with its arch origin recorded anyway. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Trapezius and cleidomastoid series
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 3. Four parts, against six in the platypus and two in a human — the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid of human anatomy are each a fusion of what is separate in most other mammals, and this row exists so the human names are not read as the primitive count. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Cucullaris (caput and hals parts)
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. cucullaris, caput part.** Although there is much fascial connection posteriorly, par- ticularly in the dorsal half of the neck, the primary origin is from the diapophysis of the fourth cervical vertebra. It is difficult to be more spe- cific regarding the origin because of the intimate relationship of fascial elements in this area. Insertion.—Anteriorly the muscle attaches to the most superficial part of the occipital crest from the midline laterad. The medial part of the insertion is immediately superficial to the insertion of M. biventer cerv., and the lateral part to the insertion of M. splenius cap.
