occurrences.name: Pectoralis thoracica
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. pectoralis.** This massive muscle is the largest in the body. The origin is fleshy from the entire ventral surface of the sternal body, the membrane overlying M. supracoracoideus, the posterior half of the sternal keel extending to its caudalmost point, and extending cranially onto the sternolateral arm of the furcula. Intermuscular lines on the sternal keel separate the origin area of this muscle from that of M. supracoracoideus, and its furcular origin is indicated by intermuscular lines and an area of rugose texture on the bone’s surface. Closer to its insertion, there is a broad area of contact between this muscle and M. coracobrachialis cranialis. The massive, mixed fleshy and tendinous insertion is on the distal cranial face of the deltopectoral crest of the humerus, where it leaves a circular, rugose scar.

homology.notes: Present in every limbed tetrapod. One of the least ambiguous rows in the comparative tables — origin, insertion, innervation and ventral-mass derivation are all congruent.
homology.teaching: Use as the anchor when introducing the ventral/flexor mass. Everything else in the ventral mass can be located relative to it.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Supracoracoideus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass, but see homology note on the mammalian supraspinatus/infraspinatus.
synonyms: 'infraspinatus' (Diogo & Abdala 2010, for the monotreme muscle Gambaryan et al. 2015 call supracoracoideus)
'supracoracoideus accessorius' (Burch 2014) = deltoideus minor (Aves) = supracoracoideus pars scapularis (Dilkes 2000) = coracobrachialis brevis dorsalis (Meers 2003)

consensus.origin: Lateral (external) surface of the coracoid and scapula, anterior/dorsal to the pectoralis origin.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, on or near the deltopectoral crest and greater tubercle.
consensus.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus. In birds, uniquely, it is the upstroke muscle.
consensus.innervation: Supracoracoid nerve; suprascapular nerve (C5–C6) in mammals.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.note: Reconstructed from the homology hypotheses of Diogo et al. (2016) as much as from the correlate: Molnar et al. list it with the procoracohumeralis as reconstructable because similar muscles are present in extant lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. An ill-defined ridge between the proximal extent of the ventral humeral ridge and the deltoid-supinator ridge, read by Andrews & Westoll (1970a) as the supracoracoideus insertion. It is one of two correlates identified in this taxon and in no other tetrapodomorph fish, which Molnar et al. flag as reason for caution. No landmark is asserted: the ridge is not one of the named correlates they carry through the character mapping.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The proximal ventral surface of the humerus divides into a smooth anterior region and a rough, concave posterior one, read as the insertions of the supracoracoideus and the coracobrachialis respectively (Coates 1996); the same configuration is described in Baphetes, Crassigyrinus, Ichthyostega, Greererpeton and Tulerpeton. Both muscles are scored as humerus/ventral, because the anterior-posterior distinction between them lies within that surface rather than being a second side, and which region each muscle took is kept here where it reads as the argument it is.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. One of the six muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct here with their highest confidence, on the strength of correlates Bishop (2014) identified; they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fan-shaped and parallel-fibred, its posterior part lying deep to the pectoralis and inserting beside it on the same crest. In salamanders the supracoracoideus is still a ventral adductor; the dorsal, wing-elevating role it takes in birds requires the triosseal canal, which does not exist here.
occurrences.origin: Ventral superficial surface of the coracoid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the humerus, adjacent to the pectoralis insertion.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Fleshy origin on the PROXIMO-LATERAL coracoid, covering the entire humeral head; fleshy insertion on the VENTRO-LATERAL humerus at the deltopectoral crest. Broad and triangular, forming much of the shoulder. Both aspects are stated by Klinkhamer et al. and both had been overwritten by the global side table, which gave coracoid/ventral and deltopectoral-crest/anterior — the one thing this source is cited for is that it names the aspect.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus complex (longus, intermedius, brevis)
occurrences.action: The primary protractors of the humerus; the brevis also adducts.
occurrences.innervation: Nerve to supracoracoideus, a branch of SN VIII, shared by all divisions.

parts.name: Supracoracoideus longus
parts.note: Fan-shaped and dominant. Extensive fleshy origin from the cranial half of the MEDIAL surface of the scapula and the adjacent coracoid opposite the glenoid.

parts.name: Supracoracoideus intermedius
parts.note: Short and thick. Its origin on the scapulocoracoid is hemmed in by those of the longus and brevis, and it inserts in common with the longus.

parts.name: Supracoracoideus brevis
parts.note: Thin. Origin on the lower portion of the LATERAL surface of the acromion, and frequently the adjacent coracoid.

occurrences.divisionNote: Meers separates three heads sharing one nerve and one insertion region. He warns the longus is the hardest to separate cleanly in dissection because the heads intermingle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator mississippiensis, from Meers (2003). The three heads have distinct origins and a shared insertion region on the deltopectoral crest: the brevis inserts just distal to the longus and immediately ventral to deltoideus clavicularis. The acromion row is the brevis origin. The Crocodylus porosus row beside this one is Klinkhamer et al.'s undivided segmentation of the same complex, which is a difference in method — CT segmentation against dissection — not a difference between the animals.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.action: Wing upstroke. The tendon is redirected over the shoulder by the triosseal canal so that a ventrally placed muscle produces a dorsal pull — the pulley arrangement that permits both flight strokes to be powered from below the body's centre of mass.
occurrences.note: = pectoralis secundus sensu Jollie (1962). In penguins the supracoracoideus is very well developed relative to the pectoralis, which Schreiweis (1982) notes every anatomist working on the group has remarked on. In a flying bird the pectoralis dwarfs it; in a wing-propelled diver, where the upstroke is also a power stroke, the two approach parity. Same two muscles, same triosseal pulley, different force balance.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar. Origin restricted to the sternal keel and the tendon rerouted dorsally through the foramen triosseum, so a ventrally placed muscle produces the upstroke.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Cranial part of the ventral surface of the procoracoid, passing through a gap between its cranial border and the interclavicle onto its dorsal side.
occurrences.insertion: Anteroproximal part of the proximal ventral surface of the humerus only, between the coracobrachialis brevis (posteriorly) and the infraspinatus (anteriorly), without reaching the anterior or dorsal sides of the greater tubercle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The attachments here are Gambaryan et al.'s m. supracoracoideus alone, which is the muscle Diogo & Abdala (2010) call the infraspinatus. The two muscles this record's synonym list treats as its mammalian halves are separate bellies in this animal and are not scored into these rows: the supraspinatus runs from the lower third of the INTERNAL surface of the scapula to the proximal apex of the greater tubercle, and the infraspinatus from the external surface of the scapula, cranial to the triceps longus crest, to the greater tubercle just distal to the supraspinatus.
occurrences.divisionNote: See the Zaglossus row on this record for the argument. Howell (1937) failed to find supracoracoid innervation for the big infraspinous muscle and renamed it teres minor, which Gambaryan et al. say destroyed the homologisation of everything around it; Westling (1889), McKay (1894) and Shrivastava (1962) all did find that nerve supply, and this paper restores their identification.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.action: Supraspinatus abducts and stabilises; infraspinatus laterally rotates.
occurrences.note: The migration of this muscle from the coracoid to the lateral scapula, and its division by the newly evolved scapular spine, is one of the defining events of the synapsid pectoral transformation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Origin has migrated off the coracoid — which no longer exists as a separate bone — onto the lateral scapula, where the new scapular spine splits it into supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin restricted to the sternal keel and the tendon rerouted dorsally through the foramen triosseum, so a ventrally placed muscle produces the upstroke.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Cranial part of the ventral surface of the procoracoid, passing through a gap between its cranial border and the interclavicle onto the dorsal side of both bones.
occurrences.insertion: Anteroproximal part of the proximal ventral surface of the humerus, anterior to the coracobrachialis brevis, then along the anterior side of the greater tubercle onto its dorsal side between the infraspinatus (proximal) and the pectoralis (distal).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Of the three genera this one alone carries the insertion over the greater tubercle and onto its dorsal face; in the short-beaked echidna it stops short of it.
occurrences.divisionNote: Three separate muscles, not two — and that is the argument. Romer (1922) derived the therian supraspinatus and infraspinatus from the supracoracoideus of lower tetrapods on the strength of shared innervation, which is the hypothesis this record's synonym list encodes. Gambaryan et al. object that in monotremes all three are present simultaneously, and read the monotreme supracoracoideus as homologous with the reptilian, avian and amphibian muscle outright, with supraspinatus and infraspinatus as mammalian additions to the group. Their membership is marked disputed on that basis rather than the record being restructured on one source.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Almost the entire ventral surface of the procoracoid, passing through a gap between its cranial border and the interclavicle slightly onto its dorsal side.
occurrences.insertion: Mostly fleshy along the dorsal — not the ventral — side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, descending from its proximal apex at the greater tubercle to the insertion of the acromiodeltoideus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The largest procoracoid origin of the three and the only insertion that runs down the pectoral crest rather than sitting on the proximal humeral surface. The supraspinatus is vestigial in this animal, restricted to the internal side of the base of the acromion, which Gambaryan et al. read as secondary reduction following the invasion of the subscapularis onto the inner face of the scapula.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.action: Protracts and slightly abducts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Two things are packed into this row.

**A functional argument breaks a phylogenetic tie.** The insertion is phylogenetically equivocal: crocodylians take it on the tip and adjacent lateral surface of the deltopectoral crest, birds on the posterior surface of the greater tubercle, and Jasinoski et al. (2006) chose the avian site for dromaeosaurids from a rugose depression in *Velociraptor*. Burch rejects it for early theropods on mechanics rather than on parsimony — the avian arrangement works through the triosseal canal, which nonavian theropods do not have, and without it a greater-tubercle insertion would be nearly non-functional. *Tawa* then supplies the positive evidence the argument wanted: a small oblong depression on the lateral surface of the deltopectoral crest immediately adjacent to its tip.

**The second part is Burch's own homology hypothesis.** He derives the avian Deltoideus minor from the supracoracoideus mass rather than the deltoid group, following Sullivan (1962) on development and topology against the innervation, and names the result Supracoracoideus accessorius — the same muscle Dilkes (2000) called Supracoracoideus pars scapularis and Meers (2003) removed from the complex entirely as Coracobrachialis brevis dorsalis. It is scored here as a disputed part rather than its own record. Its origin is the subacromial depression, shared with the supracoracoideus; its insertion is the second deltopectoral-crest row, on the proximal edge between the greater tubercle and the tip. Both are unequivocal *given* the homology, which is exactly the part that is not.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.action: Supraspinatus initiates abduction of the arm; infraspinatus laterally rotates it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Two fossae either side of the scapular spine to two facets on the greater tubercle, both on the suprascapular nerve. **That shared innervation is the entire argument for the supracoracoideus → supraspinatus + infraspinatus transformation**, and this row is what the argument is about — the scapular spine that divides them is a therian novelty, so the two fossae did not exist to be divided in any outgroup. Gambaryan et al. (2015) attack the transformation from the monotremes, where a supracoracoideus and a supraspinatus and an infraspinatus are all three present at once. Read this row against the monotreme rows on this record, not on its own.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Arises from the deep corner where the carina meets the sternal plane — the rostrum sterni — and from the Membrana sternocoracoclavicularis, the ligamentous sheet tying sternum, coracoid and furcula together, which has no element here and is carried in prose. **The insertion is the whole flight mechanism in one sentence**: the tendon passes through the canal formed by clavicle, coracoid and scapula and ends on the Tuberculum dorsale on the *caudal* surface of the proximal humerus, so a muscle lying under the bird lifts the wing. That tubercle is scored as the greater tubercle rather than as an avian element of its own; see the note on `greater-tubercle`.

**M. deltoideus minor is recorded here as a disputed part**, following Sullivan (1962) and Burch (2014), who derive it from the supracoracoideus mass rather than the deltoid group and name the result supracoracoideus accessorius; Diogo & Abdala (2010) instead make it the deltoideus clavicularis. Matsuoka & Hasegawa describe it arising from the hard ligament between the posterior tip of the coracoid head and the scapular acromion, and inserting on the dorsal slope of the same Tuberculum dorsale the supracoracoideus wraps — which is the topological adjacency the homology argument rests on.

occurrences.name: M. supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). A thick fan on the ventrolateral coracoid plate, from the anterior aspect of the epicoracoid and the ventral face of the coracoid, overlying the ventral half of the scapulocoracoid fenestra and both coracoid fenestrae, and running medially as far back as the coracosternal articulation. It tapers to a tendinous insertion on the proximal border of the deltopectoral crest. **The line separating it from the scapulohumeralis anterior marks the separation of scapula from coracoid** — a muscle boundary that is also a bone boundary, which is the sort of correspondence the whole record depends on and which therians lost with the coracoid.

occurrences.name: M. supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther called it *M. coraco-brachialis anterior*. The superficial portion is a very weak small muscle from the coracoid near its mediocephalic angle to the processus lateralis humeri; the deep portion is a very powerful mass arising from almost the entire outer surface of the coracoid and inserting both on that process and along the medial-anterior surface of the proximal two-thirds of the humeral shaft. **A long insertion down the shaft, not a tendon onto a crest** — the state this record's other columns should be read against, since in birds the same muscle has become a wing elevator working through a canal.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The supraspinatus is the bulkier of the two in all three animals** — here nearly twice as large. Cunningham is checking Meckel's claim that the infraspinatus is the smaller throughout Marsupialia, and finds it holds; he cites Macalister for the wombat, phalanger, bandicoot, *Sarcophilus* and opossum, for the two being about equal in the giant kangaroo, and for the infraspinatus being the larger in Bennett's kangaroo. That is the one reported exception, and it is not in this dataset.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **The supraspinatus is the bulkier of the two in all three animals** — here larger, though the disparity is the least of the three. Cunningham is checking Meckel's claim that the infraspinatus is the smaller throughout Marsupialia, and finds it holds; he cites Macalister for the wombat, phalanger, bandicoot, *Sarcophilus* and opossum, for the two being about equal in the giant kangaroo, and for the infraspinatus being the larger in Bennett's kangaroo. That is the one reported exception, and it is not in this dataset.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **The supraspinatus is the bulkier of the two in all three animals** — here fully three times as large. Cunningham is checking Meckel's claim that the infraspinatus is the smaller throughout Marsupialia, and finds it holds; he cites Macalister for the wombat, phalanger, bandicoot, *Sarcophilus* and opossum, for the two being about equal in the giant kangaroo, and for the infraspinatus being the larger in Bennett's kangaroo. That is the one reported exception, and it is not in this dataset.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527. Fleshy origin from the proximal half of the sternal keel, extending cranially over much of the ventral surface of the coracoid, and lying deep to the pectoralis on the keel. The thick tendon of this muscle passes through the triosseal canal and inserts on the proximal face of the dorsal tubercle of the humerus.

occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. supracoracoideus.** Fleshy origin comes from all the surfaces of the keel and the sternal plate covered by the belly (fig. 29). This extends anteriorly on to the proximal half of the anterior face of the coracoid and to the most anterior extent of the bony tracheal enclosure formed by the sternum. homology.notes: The supracoracoideus → supraspinatus + infraspinatus transformation is argued from shared suprascapular innervation, and the monotreme condition has been its main morphological support. **Gambaryan et al. (2015) attack it from exactly there.** Their objection is that in all three living monotreme genera the supracoracoideus, the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus are present AT THE SAME TIME, as three separate bellies with three separate attachments — the supracoracoideus arising from the procoracoid, a bone therians do not have, and the other two from the scapula. On their reading the monotreme supracoracoideus is homologous with the reptilian, avian and amphibian supracoracoideus outright, and supraspinatus and infraspinatus are mammalian additions to the group rather than its two halves. The intermediate this record was resting on is on their evidence not an intermediate at all. Recorded rather than acted on: the three monotreme occurrences carry supraspinatus and infraspinatus as `membership: disputed` parts, and the record is not split on one source. The avian supracoracoideus is homologous to the reptilian muscle either way; only its tendon path is novel, and nothing here touches that.
homology.openQuestion: Are the therian supraspinatus and infraspinatus subdivisions of the supracoracoideus, as Romer (1922) held and the shared innervation suggests, or mammalian additions alongside a supracoracoideus that persisted independently and was lost only in therians? Deciding it means separate `supraspinatus` and `infraspinatus` records and a re-score of the therian column, which one paper does not warrant.
homology.teaching: Two independent teaching payloads: (1) the synapsid coracoid-to-scapula migration, readable directly off the monotreme condition; (2) the avian triosseal pulley, where homology is preserved but mechanics are inverted. Third payload: compare the penguin. Schreiweis (1982) finds the supracoracoideus nearly matching the pectoralis in wing-propelled divers, against the large disparity in aerial fliers — a force-balance change with no change in homology, attachment or nerve. Fourth, and the sharpest: the monotreme condition is cited in textbooks as the transitional stage of the first payload, and the most detailed modern dissection of it says the transition is not what is being looked at. Worth handing students both claims and the same animal.

muscles.name: Deltoideus scapularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the limb bud.
synonyms: dorsal or scapular part of deltoideus (Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001)
spinodeltoideus (Gambaryan et al. 2015, who give the equivalence with deltoideus scapularis sensu Diogo & Abdala 2010 explicitly)

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula and suprascapula.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus.
consensus.action: Abducts, protracts and laterally rotates the humerus; antagonist of the pectoralis.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal (extensor) division of the brachial plexus (C5–C6).

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.note: The deltoideus is one of the four muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct in tetrapodomorph fish with their highest confidence.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Origin from the thickened posterior margin of the cleithrum just above the glenoid, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as the deltoideus plus part of the latissimus dorsi — Molnar et al. label it 'del?' and note that a comparable posterior flange in Strepsodus and Megalichthys might as easily carry an undifferentiated superficial adductor. Insertion on the dorsal humerus with no landmark: the ectepicondyle, deltoid process and possible incipient latissimus dorsi process are close together and hard to distinguish here, and Molnar et al. hold that for muscle reconstruction it does not matter whether the deltoid and supinator processes are separate, since neither reading indicates separate muscles.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The ectepicondyle, deltoid process and latissimus dorsi process are clearly separate here, unlike in Eusthenopteron where the three are close together (Vorobyeva 1995; Shubin et al. 2006; Ahlberg 2011). The insertion is still scored on the dorsal humerus without a landmark: Molnar et al. put the deltoideus insertion on the dorsal ridge and its derivatives, and Boisvert (2009) reads the deltoid and supinator processes as a continuous flange in this taxon.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from a muscle scar on the lateral surface of the cleithrum just dorsal to the anteroventral process, where the cleithrum articulates with the clavicle (Coates 1996). Molnar et al. attribute cleithral and clavicular scars to 'the deltoideus and/or latissimus dorsi' without separating the two, so this row may carry a shared scar and the latissimus dorsi occurrence records no origin at all. Insertion on the deltopectoral crest, where the deltoid and pectoral processes are united.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Longitudinally oriented, anastomosing ridges and grooves along the posterior margins of both the cleithrum and the clavicle, including the ascending process of the clavicle, read by Bishop (2014) as the deltoideus origin — two rows, because they are two bones. Comparable striations on the inner surface and ascending process of the clavicle in Crassigyrinus (Panchen 1985) and on the tip of the clavicular ascending process in Greererpeton (Godfrey 1989) suggest the same origin was general in stem tetrapods. One of the six highest-confidence reconstructions here.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.note: Corresponds to the dorsalis scapulae of Smith (1926), Howell (1937b), Romer (1944), Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006).
occurrences.attachmentNote: The fibres pass around the anterior side of the humerus to reach a ventral crest — a dorsal girdle muscle with a ventral insertion, which is what lets it elevate the humerus.
occurrences.origin: Dorsolateral surface of the suprascapular cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis scapulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. The anuran novelty is a shared tendon: the dorsalis scapulae and the latissimus dorsi CONVERGE and insert together on the lateral face of the deltopectoral crest by a common tendon, which they do not do in salamanders. The dorsal musculature between trunk and forelimb is otherwise largely similar in the two groups. Sigurdsen et al. also fix the nomenclature this record depends on: the anuran and caudate 'dorsalis scapulae' is the amniote deltoideus scapularis, while the anuran 'deltoid' is the caudate procoracohumeralis and the amniote deltoideus clavicularis.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta — Walker (1973) writes *Pseudemys scripta elegans*, the red-eared slider, which is his type species and the same animal. A triangular muscle arising from the anterior surface of the scapular prong ventral to the teres major origin, from the anterior surface of the acromion, and from the median epiplastron and adjacent entoplastron. **No insertion row**: Walker gives the origin in this passage and does not state where it ends. A turtle shoulder muscle taking a third of its origin from the shell is the kind of thing the consensus row could never have shown.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Two heads: one muscular from the anterolateral suprascapula and scapula, a second from the ventral and inner border of the clavicle, both tendinous onto the deltopectoral crest. The suprascapular head is the one that disappears in mammals with the cartilage.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Fleshy on the disto-lateral scapula, tendinous on the DORSO-LATERAL HUMERAL HEAD. Klinkhamer et al. give no deltopectoral crest for this muscle — the row formerly asserted one, against its own note. The row stops at the bone because skeleton.json resolves no humeral-head site. An elongate muscle attached along the scapula from its origin until it becomes tendinous, lying anterior to teres major.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.note: Part of the acromialis sensu Ribbing (1938); part of the deltoideus sensu Jollie (1962).

occurrences.name: Deltoideus, pars scapularis (spinous part)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Deltoideus pars scapularis, from the fascia over infraspinatus, the proximal scapular spine and the metacromion, by a broad flat tendinous fascia onto the middle of the deltoid crest just lateral to the acromial belly.
occurrences.divisionNote: No division recorded. Galictis' name — 'Deltoideus, pars scapularis (spinous part)' — is one pars named with a gloss on where it sits, not a statement that the muscle is divided in this animal. Reading the parenthesis as a second part would manufacture a differentiation event out of a synonym.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Deltoideus major, a very thin triangular muscle arising fleshy from the distal apex of the clavicle, the dorsal surface of the coracoscapular ligament and the acromial process of the scapula, converging on a short tendon that inserts on the caudodorsal humerus very close to the latissimus dorsi insertion. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade. Schreiweis names the **acromial process of the scapula** as the third origin; skeleton.json records the acromion as absent in Aves and the validator rejects it, so it is not asserted here. That is now the third source to describe an acromion in a taxon this dataset denies one — see the element's own note. The acromial process is now carried as a structured landmark: it was described in this note but stripped from the row while skeleton.json scored the acromion absent in Aves. The coracoscapular ligament has no element and stays in prose.

occurrences.name: Spinodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Edge of the craniodorsal angle of the scapula.
occurrences.insertion: By a tendon from mid-height of the scapula onto the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, between the clavodeltoideus in front and the acromiodeltoideus behind.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. give the equivalence directly: their m. spinodeltoideus is the m. dorsalis scapulae of the older literature and the m. deltoideus scapularis of Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record.

occurrences.name: Spinodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Edge of the craniodorsal angle of the scapula.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal dorsal surface of the humerus between the clavodeltoideus and the acromiodeltoideus, closer to the pectoral crest than in the long-beaked echidna.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. = m. dorsalis scapulae = m. deltoideus scapularis sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010).

occurrences.name: Spinodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Edge of the craniodorsal angle of the scapula, the origin split by the insertion of the spinotrapezius so that the cranial fibres arise over that muscle and the caudal fibres emerge from beneath it.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon on the dorsal side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, between the clavodeltoideus and the acromiodeltoideus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The only genus in which another muscle's insertion divides this one's origin, and the only one whose insertion reaches the pectoral crest rather than the proximal humeral surface.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.action: Abducts and retracts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Reconstructed in the primitive state against the avian one, and the argument is about what the supracoracoideus was doing.** In birds the origin has shifted proximally onto the acromion and the insertion distally over the lateral deltopectoral crest, because the clavicularis homolog has moved to the carpus and the scapularis takes over its role — abduction then passing to a modified supracoracoideus. None of that had happened in basal theropods, where the clavicularis keeps its primitive attachments and the supracoracoideus is not modified for abduction, so a proximal avian-style origin is unlikely; the broad, distally flaring scapula also offers the area for the crocodylian-style one. Insertion in a small area on the posterior surface of the proximal humerus just distal to the greater tubercle, where *Tawa* has a small oval depression containing striations.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, pars acromialis and pars spinata
occurrences.action: Abducts the arm; the posterior fibres extend and laterally rotate it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The acromial and spinous parts of a deltoid that is undivided at dissection; see the deltoideus clavicularis row, which carries the other part of the same human muscle and the reason for splitting it. Insertion on the deltoid tuberosity — the deltopectoral crest under its human name, and the same site the clavicular part uses.

occurrences.name: M. deltoideus major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). **Three origins, and the two named heads are the wrong way round.** The superficial major head is called the posterior head although it lies anterior to the so-called anterior head; Matsuoka & Hasegawa say so explicitly. It arises from the dorsal surface at the tip of the long apex of the furcula, just behind the tensor propatagialis origin; the deeper anterior head from the middle of the anterior end of the lateral scapula; and a small diverging tendon, the scapular anchor, from the dorsal scapula between the proscapulohumeralis attachment in front and the dorsalis scapulae behind. The insertion also divides: the major branch runs widely over the anconal surface of the Crista pectoralis with a fibrous extension along the dorsal margin of the shaft reaching half its length, the other into the depression between the humeral head and the Tuberculum dorsale.

occurrences.name: M. scapulodeltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). A flat triangular muscle fanning over scapula and suprascapula, arising from a band joining the anteroventral and posteroventral corners of the lateral suprascapular face — so its origin reaches as far forward as the acromion — and from the ossified scapula behind the scapular fenestra, with a partial origin from the dorsolateral clavicle that several other workers also report. Its motor tendon passes deep to that of the clavodeltoideus and inserts on the deltopectoral crest along a line slightly medial and posterior to it. **Two records, one crest, two parallel lines** — which is what makes the deltoid complex separable here and not in a human.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Broad origin on the lateral surface of the scapula, and insertion by the tendon it shares with the deltoideus clavicularis onto the dorsocaudal deltopectoral crest. Cranially it is overlaid by the caudal projection of the trapezius. Freitas et al. note that the origin stays on the scapula here, where in *V. exanthematicus* and the two geckos of Zaaf et al. (1999) it extends onto the suprascapula and the clavicle — Russell & Bauer report exactly that wider origin for *Iguana*, so the two dissections differ on how far forward and how far dorsally the muscle reaches. Zaaf et al. call it the scapulodeltoideus, Romão et al. (2013) the deltoideus scapularis distalis.

occurrences.name: M. dorsalis scapulae (Deltoides scapularis)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *Deltoides scapularis*, Günther's *M. deltoideus*. From the dorsal surface of the cartilaginous scapula near its medial border — partly covered there by the lateral part of the levator scapulae — running almost horizontally ventrad to the lateral side of the base of the processus lateralis humeri, where the cleido-humeralis overlies it. **The insertion is on cartilage at one end and a process at the other**, which is why the row does not resemble the mammalian deltoid.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, scapular portion
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The larger of the two deltoid portions: acromion, the whole length of the scapular spine, and the fascia over the infraspinatus, to the outer surface of a salient ridge on the antero-external humeral shaft at the junction of its upper and middle thirds. As it descends it is joined superficially by exactly those trapezius fibres that in a human go to the acromion — so in this animal the acromial deltoid and part of the trapezius are one sheet, and that composite is what Cunningham means by the cephalo-humeral muscle.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, acromial and spinal portions
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **The deltoid is triple here** — clavicular, acromial and spinal, quite separate except at their common insertion — because the acromial fibres descend as a narrow band apart from those off the scapular spine. This row carries the acromial and spinal parts. The humeral trapezius joins the clavicular deltoid alone and has no connection with the acromial part, which is the difference from the cuscus. The humeral ridge they insert on is less strongly marked than the cuscus's.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, scapular portion
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Origin as in the cuscus, but **separate from the clavicular deltoid at both ends** rather than only at the origin, and inserted higher — on the outer aspect of the shaft about an inch below the greater tubercle, above the clavicular deltoid's insertion. It receives no fibres from the trapezius, so unlike the cuscus's this part of the deltoid is not a constituent of the cephalo-humeral muscle.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus major
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. deltoideus major.** It is fleshy from the dorso-lateral surface of the scapular head, anterior to the origin of the scapular part of M. triceps, and posterior to that part of M. delt. minor which comes from the scapula. At its dorso- medial edge there is some origin from the dorsal end of the clavicle. The tendon, previously described, to the blade of the scapula might also be considered as part of the origin. Insertion —The distal end of the belly tapers to a point (fig. 18) on the anconal surface of the humerus. The insertion is thus fleshy and em- braces all of the proximal half of the anconal surface exclusive of the bicipital area and that region lying proximal to a line drawn between 58 *Insertion.* The distal end of the belly tapers to a point (fig. 18) on the anconal surface of the humerus. The insertion is thus fleshy and em- braces all of the proximal half of the anconal surface exclusive of the bicipital area and that region lying proximal to a line drawn between 58 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE the external tuberosity and the ligamental furrow. The posterior edge of the insertion is marked in the middle of its length by the wide aponeurosis which the scapular head of M. triceps sends to the anconal surface of the humerus; distally the posterior edge is next to the anterior edges of the fleshy origins of the internal and external heads of M. triceps.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus pars major
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. deltoideus pars major.** Fig. 5 Muscle origins and insertions on the humerus. A: Right humerus in cranial view, with osteological features labelled. B: Right humerus in caudal view, with osteological features labelled. C: Same as A, with muscle origins and insertions highlighted. D: Right humerus in dorsal view, with muscle origins and insertions highlighted. E: Same as B, with muscle origins and insertions highlighted. F: Right humerus in ventral view, with muscle origins and insertions highlighted. Scale bar = 40 mm. was found to be minute and threadlike, with a diameter of approximately 1mm. The origin was found to be directly caudal to that of M. scapulotriceps on the scapula, and the insertion is on the crest extending distally from the ventral tubercle, dorsal to the pneumatic foramen. There are no osteological correlates associated with this muscle. This large muscle has a fleshy origin that covers much of the lateral head of the scapula and extends onto the ventrolateral aspect of the furcular head. The fleshy insertion is broad, covering nearly all of the caudal surface of the deltopectoral crest and extending distally onto the humeral shaft. Despite its relatively large size, there are few osteological correlates associated with this muscle. A smooth area on the otherwise rugose ventral furcular head may be associated with this muscle’s origin, but no marks are present on the scapula. Some extremely faint intermuscular lines are present in some osteological specimens on the caudal deltopectoral crest.

homology.notes: Present in all six of Abdala & Diogo's columns and in mammals. Together with the deltoideus clavicularis it forms the deltoid complex; the boundary between the two varies with the degree of girdle ossification.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.
