muscles.name: Deltoideus clavicularis / procoracohumeralis
synonyms: ventral or clavicular part of deltoideus (Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Clavicle, procoracoid, or acromion.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus, anterior to the deltoideus scapularis insertion.
consensus.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.note: Reconstructable in tetrapodomorph fish on homology grounds — similar muscles are present in extant lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods — rather than from the correlate alone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. A hollow just dorsal to the glenoid on the scapulocoracoid, read as the procoracohumeralis origin — Andrews & Westoll's (1970a) 'scapulohumeralis'. The nomenclature is the substance here. Molnar et al.'s procoracohumeralis has two homologues in Iguana, the scapulohumeralis anterior from the lateral scapula and the deltoideus clavicularis from the medial clavicle, so the fossil rows on this record are the undivided ancestral muscle, and the correlate's position above the glenoid corresponds to the scapular of those two rather than the clavicular. Molnar & Diogo (2021) reach the same place from the other end: reconstructions of the deltoid group across seven fossil taxa are nearly identical, and the scapulohumeralis-versus-procoracohumeralis dispute is nomenclatural rather than anatomical.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the lateral fossa on the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the glenoid, observed by Molnar et al. on MGUH 1258 and 1300; the posterior fossa beside it carries the subcoracoscapularis. Their general reading of the stem-tetrapod girdle is that the two fossae, separated by the anterior glenoid buttress, mark two deep dorsal muscles with different lines of action. Insertion in the scapulohumeral depression of the dorsal humerus, proximal and anterior to the latissimus dorsi attachment — Coates's 'scapulohumeralis-like muscle'.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Scarring over a large, shallow concavity on the lateral face of the scapulocoracoid, read by Bishop (2014) as the procoracohumeralis origin ('scapulohumeralis'), and one of the six highest-confidence reconstructions here. The same lateral fossa is identified in Hynerpeton, in captorhinids and in Pederpes, and Molnar et al. homologise it with the facet that carries the adductor profundus origin just dorsal to the glenoid in Neoceratodus and Latimeria — the fin muscle mass this one comes out of.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.note: The amphibian name reflects the procoracoid origin; the muscle is the same field as the amniote deltoideus clavicularis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Called procoracohumeralis in amphibians purely because the origin sits on the procoracoid.
occurrences.origin: Procoracoid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior surface of the proximal humerus.

occurrences.name: Deltoid (procoracohumeralis)
occurrences.divisionNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Gaupp (1904) divided the anuran deltoid into three parts with separate origins and insertions; in Leiopelma, as in Ascaphus, it is a more unified mass with two or three heads of origin and two regions of insertion. Scored `heads` rather than `divided` for that reason, with Gaupp's names kept because Sigurdsen et al. judge his description still largely accurate even where the fibres do not follow it. The salamander's equivalent is one simple muscle from the procoracoid cartilage — this is the same muscle become complex and often massive.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Pars episternalis from the anterior epicoracoid onto the DISTAL end of the deltopectoral crest, closely associated with the underlying coracoradialis. Pars scapularis, the most robust part, from the anterior edges of the scapula and clavicle, its dorsalmost fibres from the anterior process of the scapula — a short anteriorly pointed process between the dorsal and ventral expansions, most pronounced in ranids but present here. It inserts on the deltopectoral crest, with fibres continuing more distally onto the shaft, which is the second insertion row. In Rana and Lithobates part of the deltoid also arises from the INTERIOR surface of the scapula, on a vertical ridge behind the scapular cleft that Gaupp described; that ridge is lacking or indistinct in primitive taxa, so it is not scored here.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylians have no clavicle, so despite the name the origin sits on the scapula — which is why Fürbringer (1876) called this muscle the scapularis inferior.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator mississippiensis, from Meers (2003). Superficial and parallel-fibred, lying immediately ventral to the trapezius insertion and overlying the ventral part of deltoideus scapularis and teres major. Fleshy origin from the acromion process and along the cranial margin of the scapula. The Caiman row beside this one gives the origin as lateral scapula from Abdala & Diogo's survey; Meers resolves it to the acromion, which is the finer reading of the same attachment rather than a disagreement.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. deltoideus pars minor: fleshy origin on the lateral aspect of the acrocoracoid process of the coracoid and on the acromial process of the furcula, ventral and lateral to the origin of M. deltoideus pars propatagialis. Short-bellied, inserting on the proximodorsal margin of the humeral head. **The furcular head is the point of interest** — this record is the clavicular deltoid, and the avian furcula is the fused clavicles, so the homology is carried by a bone that no longer exists as a pair. Scored on the furcula without a landmark: the 'acromial process of the furcula' is not the scapular acromion, which skeleton.json correctly records as absent in birds — the validator rejected the row on both counts. Two different structures sharing a word.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus, pars acromialis and pars scapularis
occurrences.action: Abducts and flexes the humerus.
occurrences.note: Galictis cuja. Ercoli et al. describe two bellies, pars acromialis and pars scapularis — NO pars clavicularis, and the word 'clavicle' does not occur anywhere in their 35 pages. This row previously read 'Acromion and lateral third of the clavicle' onto 'Deltoid tuberosity' with an axillary nerve of C5-C6, which is human textbook anatomy, and it was attributed to Rattus norvegicus because Campbell's rat dissection guide was cited alongside — a guide that states no attachment for any muscle. The clavicle came from this record's own NAME. Romer (1924) derived the mammalian teres minor and deltoideus clavicularis from the procoracohumeralis, against Mivart's (1869) suggestion that the subclavius came from this field; that is a homology argument and belongs to the record, not to an animal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Two bellies, neither clavicular. Pars acromialis arises by fleshy and tendinous fibres from the ACROMION and usually the distalmost base of the metacromion, inserting along the deltoid crest — the deltopectoral crest under another name. Pars scapularis arises from the fascia over the infraspinatus and the proximal region of the SCAPULAR SPINE, plus fleshy and tendinous fibres from the metacromion, and inserts by a broad flat tendinous fascia on the middle of the same crest, just lateral to the acromial belly. The metacromion is not in skeleton.json, so it is carried in prose; adding it would be worthwhile, since it is a carnivoran process that both bellies use. The muscle is renamed at every step for the bone that happens to carry its origin, though the muscle itself is continuous across Tetrapoda — which is exactly how a clavicle got written into this row.

occurrences.name: Clavodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Caudal border of the clavicle and the lateral ramus of the interclavicle, from the level of the procoracoid to the acromion.
occurrences.insertion: Widely on the anterior part of the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, including the pectoral crest.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The acromiodeltoideus is a separate muscle here, from the apex of the acromion, inserting by an aponeurosis that embraces the spinodeltoideus from behind and fuses with the clavodeltoideus above and below it.

parts.name: Acromiodeltoideus
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. note that reptiles have only two deltoid muscles, matching the clavodeltoideus and spinodeltoideus, and that the submerged position and wide humeral insertion of the acromiodeltoideus in monotremes suggest it is instead a portion of the reptilian scapulohumeralis anterior — whose deeper portion is the therian teres minor.

occurrences.name: Clavodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Entire ventral surface of the clavicle except its acromial end, and the entire ventral surface of the lateral ramus of the interclavicle, with a superficial aponeurosis over the medial quarter of its length.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, the most distal fibres by a short strong tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The acromiodeltoideus is separate, arising only from the apex of the acromion and inserting on the proximal dorsal humerus behind the clavodeltoideus and spinodeltoideus.

occurrences.name: Clavodeltoideus + acromiodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Ventral surface of the acromion, the ventral surface of the lateral ramus of the interclavicle, and the clavicle as far medially as the sternomastoideus insertion.
occurrences.insertion: Descends along the pectoral crest of the humerus and far distal to it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The two deltoids are inseparable here and together embrace the spinodeltoideus from below; the fibres caudal to it can be called acromiodeltoideus and those cranial to it clavodeltoideus, but there is no boundary. Diogo & Abdala (2010) do not list an acromiodeltoideus for this animal at all.
occurrences.divisionNote: `heads` rather than `divided` against both echidnas, which is a real difference and not a reading of the same thing: in Tachyglossidae the two are distinct muscles with separate origins and insertions, and in the platypus they are one continuous sheet whose parts are named by where they sit relative to the spinodeltoideus.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.action: Abducts and slightly protracts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). The avian homolog is Propatagialis, on Sullivan (1962) and Howell (1937) for its development out of the deltoid group. Burch rejects two rival homologies in passing: Diogo & Abdala's (2010) equation of Deltoideus clavicularis with the avian Deltoideus minor (which he assigns to the supracoracoideus mass — see supracoracoideus), and Meers's (2003) equation of Propatagialis with the crocodylian Humeroradialis, for which he finds no evidence beyond a shared deltoid derivation and which fails on both attachments.

**The furcula row is scored on a bone not preserved in this animal.** Birds take part of this origin from the furcula and lepidosaurs from the clavicle, which implies independent loss in modern crocodylians; furculae are known for many theropods including *Coelophysis*, so Burch extends the origin onto a hypothetical furcula in *Tawa*. The acromial row is firmer: the origin is nearly linear along the anterodorsal edge of the acromion process in every extant taxon Burch studied, with no extension onto the lateral scapula below it — which is where Jasinoski et al. (2006) put it, in the subacromial depression. Insertion broadly on the lateral surface of the deltopectoral crest, posterior to the supracoracoideus musculature, with a low ridge in *Tawa* marking its posterior limit — the same ridge that gives the lateral head of triceps its origin.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, pars clavicularis
occurrences.action: Flexes and medially rotates the arm; assists abduction.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The human deltoid is one muscle in dissection and two records here**, and the split is not arbitrary: the clavicular part is the procoracohumeralis/deltoideus clavicularis of the outgroups and the acromial and spinous parts are the deltoideus scapularis, so a single human belly spans two homology groups that are separate muscles in a lizard. Gest gives the whole muscle one origin line — lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, lower lip of the crest of the scapular spine — and one insertion, the deltoid tuberosity, which is the human name for the deltopectoral crest. Both halves therefore carry the same insertion row, which is the honest representation of a fused insertion rather than a duplication.

occurrences.name: M. clavodeltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). From the medial half of the clavicle by two fibre groups whose arrangement inverts on the way to the humerus: the ventral, superficial group winds around the anterior margin of the clavicle and emerges along its posterior border as the *dorsal* part of the muscle, while the deeper group from the dorsal clavicle passes straight back. Insertion anterodorsally on the deltopectoral crest with the scapulodeltoideus, and it is not linear — the fibres arising nearest the glenoid insert most proximally.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). **Origin from the middle portion of the interclavicle** — a different bone from the clavicle Russell & Bauer give for the same animal, and the clearest disagreement between the two dissections. Thin and elongate on the medioventral face of the girdle. Its fibres converge with those of the deltoideus scapularis onto a tendon the two muscles share, reaching the dorsocaudal surface of the deltopectoral crest; Freitas et al. report that same shared tendon in *Lacerta agilis exigua* and *V. exanthematicus* after Romer (1944) and Jenkins & Goslow (1983), and read it as a purchase that helps stabilise the forelimb in a climbing animal. Zaaf et al. (1999) call this muscle the clavodeltoideus and Romão et al. (2013) the deltoideus scapularis proximalis.

occurrences.name: M. cleido-humeralis (Deltoides clavicularis)
occurrences.innervation: Terminal branch of the N. dorsalis scapulae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *Deltoides clavicularis*, Günther's *musculus clavicolo-brachialis*. It lies between the pectoralis and the dorsalis scapulae, arises from the outer surface of the large lateral part of the clavicle, and inserts on the proximal humerus **lateral to the processus lateralis humeri** — beside the pectoralis insertion rather than on it. Compare the *Iguana* row from Russell & Bauer, where the same muscle is the clavodeltoideus and ends on the deltopectoral crest.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, clavicular portion
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. From the middle third of the clavicle, reinforced by those trapezius fibres that in a human are attached to the clavicle, to the summit of the humeral ridge — where it fuses to some extent with the pectoralis major insertion. Separated from the scapular portion above by a considerable interval.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, clavicular portion
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The clavicular head of a triple deltoid, and **the sole recipient of the humeral trapezius fibres** in this animal. Insertion as in the cuscus, on a less prominent ridge.

occurrences.name: Deltoid, clavicular portion
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus, and the muscle in which this animal's vestigial clavicle is buried. **Three sources of fibres**: the trapezius, the cleido-mastoid, and — only in part — the lower border of the vestigial clavicle itself. So the bone contributes least to the muscle named after it. Inserted into a ridge on the antero-external shaft about its middle, below the scapular deltoid and partly fused with the pectoralis major. Cunningham's cephalo-humeral muscle in this animal is this muscle plus the cleido-mastoid plus the anterior trapezius; the acromial deltoid is not part of it, as it is in the cuscus.

homology.notes: Continuous across Tetrapoda; the name changes with the girdle element that carries the origin (procoracoid in amphibians, clavicle/acromion in amniotes), not with the muscle's identity.
homology.teaching: A clean example of a muscle renamed for its bony origin rather than for any change in the muscle itself — exactly the kind of synonymy the comparative tables exist to dissolve.

muscles.name: Scapulohumeralis anterior
synonyms: teres minor (Gambaryan et al. 2015, for the monotreme muscle Diogo & Abdala 2010 call scapulohumeralis anterior)

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula, anteroventral to the glenoid.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus near the greater tubercle.
consensus.action: Protracts and laterally rotates the humerus; stabilises the glenohumeral joint.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis anterior
occurrences.note: = scapulohumeralis cranialis sensu Dilkes (2000) and Maxwell & Larsson (2007).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. scapulohumeralis cranialis, a thin cord between scapula and humerus with a fleshy origin and insertion. It arises on the lateral surface of the scapular neck, cranial to the origin of the lateral head of M. subscapularis, and inserts on the proximal humerus at the distal edge of the pneumatic foramen. The scapular neck and the pneumatic foramen have no elements of their own here, so both ends are scored at bone level with the detail in this note.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis cranialis
occurrences.note: Gavia immer, and the interesting thing about this row is that it disagrees with itself BETWEEN TWO SPECIMENS OF ONE SPECIES. McKitrick found the muscle ABSENT in CM 2320 — the specimen every other Gavia immer row in this dataset is scored from — and PRESENT in USNM 504983, where it is a tiny parallel-fibred muscle from a short tendon on the dorsolateral surface of the scapular head, inserting on the medial surface of the humeral head at the crus ventrale fossae between the two heads of origin of the humerotriceps. Sanders (1967) also found it in G. immer. It is present in G. stellata and relatively larger in Pelecanoides garnoti, where the origin extends onto the proximal scapular blade. Scored `uncertain` rather than `yes` or `no` because the disagreement is within the species and neither specimen can stand for it; the alternative — taking CM 2320 as the exemplar because the rest of the rows do — would turn one dissection into an avian absence. No attachments are scored: the animal they were seen in is not the animal the rest of these rows describe.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the humerus.
occurrences.note: Romer (1924) derived teres minor from the procoracohumeralis field rather than from scapulohumeralis anterior; the two hypotheses have not been decisively separated.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Teres minor, from the caudal margin of the scapula and sometimes by fascia from infraspinatus, by a thin tendon onto the lateral aspect of the base of the greater tuberosity just distal to the infraspinatus insertion. Absent on both sides of one of the six specimens, which is the kind of intraspecific absence `variable` exists for.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: A notch in the cranial border of the scapula between the acromion and the shoulder joint, and partly from the joint capsule.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy in a fossa on the dorsal side of the LESSER tubercle of the humerus, immediately anterior to the subscapularis insertion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. identify this as the m. scapulohumeralis anterior of Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record. The insertion is the point: instead of taking the therian teres minor's short route from scapula to greater tubercle, it passes postaxially beneath the triceps longus to the lesser tubercle beside the subscapularis. Compare the Galictis row on this record, which inserts on the greater tubercle.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: A notch in the cranial border of the scapula between the acromion and the shoulder joint, and partly from the joint capsule.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy in a fossa on the dorsal side of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, immediately anterior to the subscapularis insertion.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Gambaryan et al. read this muscle as the posteromedial (postaxial) subdivision of the lizard m. scapulohumeralis anterior and the therian teres minor as the anterolateral subdivision of the same mass — which is a third position on this record's open question, alongside the amniote-wide hypothesis and Romer's (1924) derivation of teres minor from the procoracohumeralis. Shrivastava (1962) took a fourth: that the true homologue of the therian teres minor is fused inseparably into the monotreme infraspinatus.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: External side of the scapula just anterior to the triceps longus profundus — a fossa for the fleshy fibres with a ridge along its anterior border for the aponeurosis — and partly from the articular capsule of the shoulder joint.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy in a fossa on the dorsal side of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, immediately anterior to the subscapularis insertion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The one genus of the three whose origin has moved off the cranial border onto the lateral face of the scapular blade, and it leaves an osteological correlate: a fossa with a bounding ridge.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis anterior
occurrences.action: Retracts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Both bracketing taxa in this dataset have lost it.** The muscle is absent in extant crocodylians and in ratites, and is reconstructed from its presence in other birds including tinamous and in lepidosaurs — so the archosaur bracket that makes the rest of this column unusually good is the one thing that does not support this row. Of the two lepidosaur parts, only the short-fibred one is reconstructed; the long-fibred part is absent in chameleons in association with increased humeral mobility, which Burch takes to apply to theropods too. The origin is a weak fossa on the posteroventral scapular blade dorsal to the triceps scapularis insertion — present in *Herrerasaurus* (PVSJ 53) and *Sanjuansaurus* (PVSJ 605), not in *Tawa*, and not the small oval rugosity Jasinoski et al. (2006) used in dromaeosaurids, which no early theropod has. **The insertion has no osteological correlate at all** in nonavian theropods — birds mark it with a pneumatic fossa — and is positioned by topology alone, just distal and lateral to the scapulohumeralis posterior insertion and medial to the ridge running down the posterior side of the proximal humerus.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Upper two-thirds of the lateral scapular border to the lowest facet of the greater tubercle. **Scored here on a correspondence the record calls proposed and unresolved**, and there are at least four positions on it: the scapulohumeralis anterior → teres minor equation used here; Romer's (1924) derivation of teres minor from the procoracohumeralis instead; Gambaryan et al.'s (2015) reading of the two as sister subdivisions of one reptilian muscle rather than one being the other; and their further suggestion that the acromiodeltoideus is a third portion of the same mass. The axillary nerve this row carries is what the deltoid group and teres minor share, and is the reason the question is live at all.

occurrences.name: M. scapulohumeralis cranialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). M. proscapulohumeralis of George & Berger. A pink, thick, short muscle from the postglenoid area of the lateral scapula, just cranial to where the scapular anchor of deltoideus major attaches, inserting on the basal area of the Crus dorsale fossae. **The two scapulohumerales insert on the two bars of the same fossa**, dorsal and ventral, which is the clearest statement in this paper of why they are two muscles and not one. Whether this muscle corresponds to the mammalian teres minor is unresolved — see this record's assessment, which now has four positions on it.

occurrences.name: M. scapulohumeralis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Two areas of origin on the scapula — a long-fibred superficial part from the ventrolateral scapula at the border of the scapulocoracoid fenestra, and a short-fibred part from the dorsal buttress of the glenoid — converging on a stout motor tendon that passes deep to the lateral scapulohumeral ligament and closely invests the joint capsule. Insertion on the posterodorsal proximal humerus, just distal to the articular capsule and proximal to the latissimus dorsi insertion. Whether this muscle corresponds to the mammalian teres minor is the unresolved question on this record; the lizard row is one of the two ends of it.

occurrences.name: M. scapulo-humeralis profundus
occurrences.innervation: N. scapulo-humeralis, from the N. dorsalis scapulae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's name. A fairly strong muscle overlain by the cleido-humeralis, bordering the supracoracoideus ventrally and the teres dorsally, from near the cephalic border of the bony scapula and the adjoining part of the coracoid, inserting on the radial-posterior part of the proximal humeral end. Whether this record corresponds to the mammalian teres minor is its standing open question; note that Osawa scores a separate *teres major* on the next record, so the tuatara has both.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.innervation: A small twig from the circumflex nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Distinct from the infraspinatus, arising from a small part of the scapula's axillary border close to the glenoid and inserting on the outer and posterior aspect of the humerus immediately below the greater tubercle. **Cunningham identifies it by its nerve**: a small twig from the circumflex (axillary), traced in both animals. That is the same criterion by which he scores it absent in the phascogale.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.innervation: A small twig from the circumflex nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Distinct from the infraspinatus, arising from a small part of the scapula's axillary border close to the glenoid and inserting on the outer and posterior aspect of the humerus immediately below the greater tubercle. **Cunningham identifies it by its nerve**: a small twig from the circumflex (axillary), traced in both animals. That is the same criterion by which he scores it absent in the phascogale.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **Absent, and absent on nerve evidence rather than on failure to find it.** Cunningham looked for the part of the infraspinatus that might be supposed to represent it and could trace no twig of the circumflex nerve into any of it — so there is no muscle here answering to the teres minor by the criterion that identified it in the thylacine and the cuscus. This is a claim about one phascogale, not about Dasyuridae: Cunningham reports Macalister finding the muscle inseparable from the infraspinatus in the giant kangaroo, the brushtail possum, the bandicoot and the Virginian opossum, distinct in the wallaby, and reduced to a fascial band in the wombat and the Tasmanian devil.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis cranialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. scapulohumeralis cranialis.** This muscle was not visible in our CT dataset, and it was listed as vestigial or absent by Livezey and Zusi (2006). Upon dissection of the stained specimen, this muscle Fig. 4 Digitally segmented osteology and myology of the coracoid and caudal humerus of Chauna torquata. A: right humerus and coracoid. B: same as A, with Mm. deltoideus minor, deltoideus major, supracoracoideus, and humerotriceps added. C: same as B, with Mm. coracobrachialis caudalis, latissimus dorsi, and scapulotriceps added. D: same as B, with Mm. subscapularis, subcoracoideus, and scapulohumeralis caudalis added. Scale bar = 40 mm. Anatomical atlas of the wing of Chauna 7

homology.notes: Patchy distribution (lepidosaurs and birds, absent in turtles, crocodylians and amphibians) makes the amniote-wide homology hypothesis weak. The correspondence with mammalian teres minor is proposed but unresolved — see the competing Romer (1924) derivation from procoracohumeralis. **Monotremes now put four positions on the board rather than two.** Gambaryan et al. (2015) identify this muscle in all three living genera, call it the teres minor, and read it as the posteromedial (postaxial) subdivision of the lizard scapulohumeralis anterior with the therian teres minor as the anterolateral subdivision of the same mass — so the two are sister portions rather than one being the other. They separately suggest the acromiodeltoideus is a third portion of that same reptilian muscle. Shrivastava (1962) held instead that the true homologue of the therian teres minor is fused inseparably into the monotreme infraspinatus. The monotreme rows carry the attachment evidence that bears on this: the muscle inserts on the LESSER tubercle beside the subscapularis, having passed postaxially beneath the triceps longus, where the therian teres minor takes the short route to the greater tubercle — which is what the Galictis row on this record shows.
homology.openQuestion: Is scapulohumeralis anterior a single retained muscle with multiple losses, or independently differentiated in lepidosaurs and birds? And is the therian teres minor the same muscle, a sister subdivision of it, or something derived from the procoracohumeralis instead?

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula posterodorsal to the glenoid.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus.
consensus.action: Retracts and laterally rotates the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Abdala & Diogo mark this cell '– [but see text]' — absent in Timon lepidus but discussed as possibly present in other lepidosaurs.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.note: = scapulohumeralis caudalis sensu Meers (2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Origin on the proximo-lateral and posterior scapula, insertion on the proximo-lateral humeral head, both fleshy. Klinkhamer et al. equate it with teres minor, which bears on the unresolved scapulohumeralis/teres minor question.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. scapulohumeralis caudalis, substantially larger than the cranialis. Its fleshy origin runs along the lateral scapula from the caudal margin of the cranialis origin to the caudal end of the bone; its thick insertion tendon passes ventral to the cranialis and spreads widely across the ventral margin of the proximal bicipital crest of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Extensive origin from about the posterior two-thirds of the dorsal and lateral scapular surfaces; the fibres pass obliquely forward to a strong tendon inserting on the posterior border of the humerus at about a third of its length. Schreiweis notes it is a very uniform muscle across the Spheniscidae. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.action: Retracts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). The lateral origin — the posteroventral part of the lateral surface of the scapular blade — is shared by crocodylians and birds, and *Struthio* restricts it to a narrow strip near the glenoid that closely matches the crocodylian condition. **The medial row is the equivocal one, and it is also the fossa another worker gave to another muscle.** In crocodylians the origin wraps around the posteroventral edge onto the area ventral to the medial scapular ridge; *Tawa* has a similarly small area there, so Burch extends the origin onto it. Jasinoski et al. (2006) read that same ventral fossa as the subscapularis origin — see the subcoracoscapularis row, which records the disagreement from the other side. Insertion on the posterior surface of the internal tuberosity, restricted as in birds rather than extensive as in some crocodylians, with an oval depression there in *Tawa* to mark it.

occurrences.name: M. scapulohumeralis caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Called M. dorsalis scapulae by George & Berger, which is a name this dataset also carries as an old synonym of the latissimus dorsi and of the deltoideus scapularis — three muscles, one discarded name. Arises widely from the lateral surface of the scapular blade, its cranial part running deep to the scapulohumeralis cranialis origin as far as the caudal margin of the glenoid, and inserts on a small notch on the caudal surface of the Crus ventrale fossae, the ventral bar of the pneumotricipital fossa — scored as `humerus[posterior]`, since the crura of that fossa are not elements here.

occurrences.note: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Scored uncertain because the source says it is not a separate muscle in this animal, not that it is absent.** Russell & Bauer state plainly that the M. scapulohumeralis posterior does not exist as a separate entity in *Iguana*, while identifying a small ventrolateral head of the M. subcoracoscapularis as its homologue — a head that is entirely scapulohumeral in extent, bridges the scapular triceps tendon and crosses the anterodorsal shoulder joint. They keep it inside the subcoracoscapularis because of how weakly developed it is and because recognising the bundle as a muscle is uncertain in general. It is scored as a disputed part on that record. A homology group that is present as tissue and absent as a muscle.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. scapulohumeralis caudalis.** The origin is fleshy and extends down the distal three quarters of the lateral scapular blade. The origin is marked by a rugose area on the lateral scapula, bounded by intermuscular lines and a proximal rugose tubercle. It extends ventrally as a broad sheet of muscle before narrowing to a tendon, which inserts as a wide sheet on the crus ventrale of the humerus and leaves an oval rugose scar.

homology.notes: An archosaur muscle on the sampling in Abdala & Diogo (2010). Widely used in archosaur fossil muscle reconstruction because it leaves a scar posterodorsal to the glenoid.

consensus.origin: Medial (internal) surface of the scapula and coracoid.
consensus.insertion: Lesser tubercle / medial process of the proximal humerus.
consensus.action: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus; a principal glenohumeral stabiliser.
consensus.innervation: Subscapular nerves (C5–C7).

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain rather than inferred. Molnar et al. report that they 'did not find compelling evidence' that the subcoracoscapularis, the coracobrachialis, the latissimus dorsi, the triceps or the individual forearm muscles existed as SEPARATE muscles in early tetrapodomorph fish, though Andrews & Westoll (1970a) reconstructed all of them. The first individual correlate of this muscle appears one node crownward, at Elpistostegalia; under their alternative phylogeny, later still, at Acanthostega and crownward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. A small mark on the posterior border of the scapulocoracoid, suggested by Andrews & Westoll (1970a) as a possible origin. Molnar et al. note that it is topologically consistent with the fossa or rugose area that carries the subcoracoscapularis in stem tetrapods, sitting beside the glenoid near the junction of the scapular and coracoid regions.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Tiktaalik roseae. Molnar et al.'s character mapping puts the first individual osteological correlate of the subcoracoscapularis at this node — a triangular region on the scapulocoracoid dorsal and posterior to the glenoid — but what they report on the specimen itself, the MCZ cast of NUFV 112, is fainter: rugosities above the glenoid and a hollow above the coracoid foramen, 'well placed for the origins of deep dorsal musculature' and not assigned to a muscle. Under the Ahlberg et al. (2008) phylogeny the maximum-likelihood reconstruction delays the correlate to Acanthostega and crownward. Hence uncertain, and no attachment row.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the posterior fossa on the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the glenoid (MGUH 1258, 1300); insertion on a process on the posterior edge of the humerus just proximal to the ectepicondyle, scarred on its ventral surface (Coates 1996), which Coates held homologous with 'process 2' of Ichthyostega. Where both a recess and a process are present, as in Crassigyrinus, Panchen (1985) read them as the insertions of separate subcoracoideus and subscapularis muscles — the division this record holds as one homology group.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Scarring over the entire posterior face of the scapulocoracoid above the glenoid and much of its internal aspect, read by Bishop (2014) as the origin of the subcoracoscapularis ('subscapularis'). The same posterior fossa or triangular region is identified in Tulerpeton, Archeria, captorhinids and Pederpes, and as the 'supraglenoid fossa' of Eryops. Molnar et al. rate the reconstruction fairly confident once the character mapping is combined with the scars.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Reported in urodeles by Smith (1926), Romer (1944) and Kardong (2002), but Abdala & Diogo flag the identification as needing confirmation.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: = subscapularis sensu Ecker (1889).

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.note: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Sigurdsen et al. state that the subscapularis of salamanders, which inserts on the humeral dorsal process, HAS NO CLEAR HOMOLOGUE IN FROGS, and they account for the one report of it in an anuran — Ritland's (1955b) subcoracoscapularis in Ascaphus — as the longus slip of the coracobrachialis under another name. Scored `no` for this species against Abdala & Diogo's `yes` for Rhinella arenarum, which makes Anura compute as `variable`. That is the disagreement, not a resolution of it: two sources, two frogs, and a muscle whose anuran presence turns on whether a coracobrachialis slip is being counted twice.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: = subscapularis + subcoracoideus sensu Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000).

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.action: Medially rotates the humerus; anterior stabiliser of the shoulder (rotator cuff).
occurrences.note: The coracoid contribution is lost with the coracoid itself; only the scapular head persists in therians.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The coracoid head is gone with the coracoid itself; only the scapular head persists, which is why the mammalian muscle is 'subscapularis' rather than 'subcoraco-scapularis'.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Both heads of this field. The subscapularis caput mediale arises from the proximal third of the costal scapula, a small area of the scapular process of the clavicle and the medial coracoid; the subcoracoideus from the dorsal spina externa of the sternum and the adjacent corpus sterni, further attaching to the dorsomedial coracoid. The two **fuse near the shoulder joint and insert by a common tendon**, which is why one record carries them. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Subscapularis from the EXTERNAL surface of the scapula caudal to the crest for the triceps longus, from the caudal border, and from a narrow strip of the internal surface along it; subcoracoideus from the dorsal (internal) surfaces of the procoracoid and coracoid, bifurcating along two longitudinal crests on the procoracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Subscapularis, bipennate, on the proximal apex of the lesser tubercle of the humerus; subcoracoideus tendinous, descending from the lesser tubercle along its crest between the coracobrachialis brevis below and the teres major above.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Both heads are present, which is the plesiomorphic amniote condition this record's name describes and which therians lost with the coracoid. The subscapularis origin is the finding: it is on the OUTER face of the scapular blade, the inverse of the therian arrangement, and the inner face is taken instead by the supraspinatus and the serratus ventralis cervicis.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Subscapularis from the external surface of the scapula caudal to the triceps longus crest, the caudal border, and a narrow strip of the internal surface; subcoracoideus from the dorsal surfaces of the procoracoid and coracoid, reaching the caudal angle of the coracoid where it fuses with the coracobrachialis brevis origin.
occurrences.insertion: Subscapularis on the proximal apex of the lesser tubercle of the humerus; subcoracoideus along the crest of the lesser tubercle between the coracobrachialis brevis and the teres major.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Gambaryan et al. regard this arrangement — subscapularis outside, supraspinatus and serratus ventralis cervicis inside — as the most primitive in mammals and probably in all synapsids, noting the half-external subscapularis that turns up in the giant anteater. The subcoracoideus tendon slides over the apex of the lesser tubercle, which carries hyaline cartilage and a synovial capsule for it.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Subscapularis in two incompletely fused heads — a laterocaudal head, twice the bulk, from the caudal border and caudal external surface of the scapula, and a medial head covering the internal surface between the two portions of the serratus ventralis cervicis; subcoracoideus from the entire dorsal surface of the procoracoid but for a narrow medial strip, its origin completely fused with that of the coracobrachialis brevis at the procoracoid-coracoid boundary.
occurrences.insertion: Subscapularis by two aponeuroses onto the proximal apex of the lesser tubercle, the medial head onto a sesamoid bone there and the laterocaudal head onto the tubercle just distal to it; subcoracoideus by four flat overlying tendons onto the lesser tubercle and its crest.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The subscapularis has begun to invade the internal face of the scapula here, which Gambaryan et al. read as the derived state and as the cause of the reduction of the supraspinatus in this animal. A sesamoid sits in the medial head's tendon at the apex of the lesser tubercle, joined to it by a synovial joint; the most proximal of the four subcoracoideus tendons inserts on that sesamoid rather than on bone, so no attachment row is written for it. Howell (1937) could not separate subcoracoideus from coracobrachialis brevis in this animal and called the mass together the m. coracobrachialis profundus, having found only the ventral nerve supply.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis and subcoracoideus
occurrences.action: Subscapularis retracts and rotates the humerus; subcoracoideus adducts and laterally rotates it.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **The origin is the one Burch calls unequivocal** — the medial surface of the scapular blade. *Tawa* has a distinct ridge there running along the proximal half to two-thirds of the scapula, and the reading of that ridge is a live disagreement worth recording: Jasinoski et al. (2006) took a similar ridge in *Meleagris* as the dorsal edge of the subscapularis origin and inferred an origin ventral to it in dromaeosaurids, but Burch notes the same ridge is present in crocodylians, where the ventral fossa it creates belongs to the scapulohumeralis posterior instead. A correlate that two workers read as bounding different muscles. In *Tawa* the ridge is ventrally shifted and meets the posteroventral edge less than half-way along the blade, leaving so little area below it that Burch puts this typically large muscle dorsally.

**Subcoracoideus is scored as a second part of the same group.** It is not an independent muscle in crocodylians, where it is fused to subscapularis, but birds and lepidosaurs give it a separate insertion, so it can be reconstructed as distinct in theropods. Its origin is unknown in extent and is placed, following Jasinoski et al. (2006), as a small area covering the coracoid foramen. Both parts share one insertion tendon on the internal tuberosity — which is why the two make one row here and not two.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.action: Medially rotates the arm; assists extension.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial two-thirds of the costal surface of the scapula to the lesser tubercle. **The human condition is the group with one of its two parts gone**: therians have no coracoid, so the subcoracoideus half of this record has nothing to arise from and the muscle is a subscapularis only. Compare the *Tawa* row on this record, where the two are separate bellies sharing one insertion tendon, and the crocodylian condition, where they are fused but both present.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Arises widely from the cranial three-fifths of the medial surface of the scapula and inserts by a strong tendon on the proximal slope of the Tuberculum ventrale. **Only one belly is scored because only one was found**: Matsuoka & Hasegawa take this to be M. subscapularis pars interna and state that they were unable to recognise a pars externa, which is a stated absence rather than an unexamined one. The Tuberculum ventrale is the lesser tubercle under Baumel's avian nomenclature — the same site the human subscapularis uses, which is only visible as the same site because the two were merged into one element.

occurrences.name: M. subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). The muscle occupies almost the entire internal surface of the scapulocoracoid, divided by the course of the medial scapulosternal ligament into a dorsolateral scapular portion and a much more extensive ventromedial coracoid portion. The coracoid head roofs all the scapulocoracoid fenestrae and takes partial origin from the fibrous sheets closing them — a muscle arising from the holes in a bone as much as from the bone. Both converge on one stout tendon onto the posterodorsal aspect of the humeral head.

**The third head is where a whole record goes.** A smaller head lies deep to the confluence of the other two, entirely scapulohumeral, bridging the tendon of origin of the scapular triceps head and crossing the anterodorsal shoulder joint. Russell & Bauer identify it as the equivalent of the M. scapulohumeralis posterior and then decline to give it that status, treating it as a part of this muscle because of its level of development and the general uncertainty over recognising the fibre bundle as a distinct muscle at all. It is scored here as a disputed part, and the `scapulohumeralis-posterior` row for this animal records the same judgement from the other side.

occurrences.name: M. subscapulo-coraco-brachialis
occurrences.innervation: N. subscapulo-coraco-brachialis, the coracoid head also receiving a branch of the N. coraco-brachialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *M. subcoraco-scapularis*, and this record's own name is the same compound. Caput scapulare from the caudal border of the bony scapula slightly ventral to the serratus superficialis insertion; caput coracoides very powerful and **doubly pennate**, from the whole dorsal surface of the coracoid except its medial and caudal borders. The two unite near their insertion on the processus medialis humeri, proximal to the medial head of the anconaeus, and Osawa notes the muscle reinforces the dorsal capsular wall of the shoulder joint. Compare the human row, where the coracoid half of this group has nothing to arise from.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Cunningham gives this muscle one sentence — well marked in all three, with the usual attachments — and no origin or insertion of his own. **No attachments are scored, because he recorded none**; copying the consensus row here would assert an observation he did not make. What he does record is a relation: its posterior border is bound to the teres major by an intermuscular septum that gives fibres to both muscles.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Cunningham gives this muscle one sentence — well marked in all three, with the usual attachments — and no origin or insertion of his own. **No attachments are scored, because he recorded none**; copying the consensus row here would assert an observation he did not make. What he does record is a relation: its posterior border is bound to the teres major by an intermuscular septum that gives fibres to both muscles.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Cunningham gives this muscle one sentence — well marked in all three, with the usual attachments — and no origin or insertion of his own. **No attachments are scored, because he recorded none**; copying the consensus row here would assert an observation he did not make. What he does record is a relation: its posterior border is bound to the teres major by an intermuscular septum that gives fibres to both muscles.

occurrences.name: Proscapulohumeralis + subscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. proscapulohumeralis and M. subscapularis.** —The proscapulohumeral part arises fleshily from the ventral edge of the second and third fifths of the length of the scapular blade and from the ventral half of the lateral face of the second fifth of the MUSCLES OF THE WING 53 scapula. M. subscap. takes fleshy origin from most of the width of the medial surface of this bone in the second and third fifths of its length. Insertion.—Distal to the tendon of insertion of M. serr. ant. it is im- possible to distinguish two separate bellies, and their insertion is, there- fore, in common. The insertion is primarily tendinous, but with some fleshy attachments, on the posterior borde *Insertion.* Distal to the tendon of insertion of M. serr. ant. it is im- possible to distinguish two separate bellies, and their insertion is, there- fore, in common. The insertion is primarily tendinous, but with some fleshy attachments, on the posterior border of the proximal one-half of the capital groove on the anconal surface of the humerus and extending on to the internal tuberosity anterior and dorsal to the insertion of M. subcoracoid. There is strong, almost tendinous, fascial connection between the deep, distal part of the belly and the underlying ribs 2 and 3. This might be considered a part of the insertion.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. subscapularis.** This muscle has a wide, fleshy origin on the ventral and medial proximal scapula, extending from the scapular head down approximately one third of the scapular blade. Faint intermuscular lines associated with this muscle's origin are visible on the ventrolateral scapula, but none exist on the medial scapula. The insertion is located on the proximal face of the ventral tubercle of the humerus via a shared tendon with M. subcoracoideus, which together leave a circular rugose area on the bone at the site of insertion. **M. subcoracoideus.** The origin is a thin strip on the lateral side of the sternal end of the dorsal face of the coracoid, extending from the lateral process to approximately halfway up the coracoid shaft. Faint intermuscular lines are present on the dorsal shaft of this bone. This muscle inserts on the humerus via a shared tendon with M. subscapularis.

homology.notes: Consistent across Tetrapoda. The 'subcoraco-' prefix records the coracoid head present wherever a coracoid persists; its loss in therians is a consequence of girdle reduction, not of muscle loss.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.
