muscles.name: Teres major
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Frequently differentiates in association with the latissimus dorsi.

consensus.origin: Posterior (caudal) border and inferior angle of the scapula.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, adjacent to or shared with the latissimus dorsi insertion.
consensus.action: Retracts, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Lower subscapular / thoracodorsal nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Origin on the anterior surface of roughly the dorsal half of the scapular prong and the suprascapular cartilage. It and the latissimus dorsi develop from one muscle mass and converge on a **common tendon** onto the dorsal humerus just distal to the head, so the insertion is shared rather than separate. Walker notes the degree of separation between the two is highly variable between turtles — absent in *Dermochelys*, incipient in *Testudo*, large in trionychids and pleurodires — so this is a row about *Trachemys* and emphatically not about Testudines.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]' by Abdala & Diogo.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Origin fleshy on the DISTO-LATERAL scapula, forming its postero-lateral surface and lying deep to the latissimus dorsi; a long well-defined tendon to a bony ridge on the proximo-lateral humerus — a scar worth looking for in fossil pseudosuchians. The origin formerly carried the SUBSCAPULAR FOSSA, which is a medial site and is not mentioned by Klinkhamer et al. anywhere; their word is disto-lateral, as this note always said.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.action: Adducts, extends and medially rotates the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the aponeurosis covering subscapularis and immediately ventral to the caudal angle of the scapula, by a wide thin tendinous fascia onto the proximal medial humeral diaphysis.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: External side of the apex of the caudal angle of the scapula, extending slightly onto its internal side below the serratus ventralis insertions.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the distal part of the crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, between the subcoracoideus insertion and the triceps accessorius origin.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: External side of the apex of the caudal angle of the scapula and also its internal side, wedging between the insertions of the serratus ventralis cervicis in front and the serratus ventralis thoracis behind.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the distal part of the crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, between the subcoracoideus insertion and the triceps accessorius origin.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The insertion is on the crest and not the apex of the lesser tubercle, which is the subscapularis' — the two are scored as separate landmarks because keeping them apart is the observation.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: Along the external side of the caudal half of the dorsal border of the scapula, up to the apex of the caudal angle where the serratus ventralis thoracis inserts.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the distal part of the crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, between the subcoracoideus insertion and the triceps accessorius origin.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The origin has spread forward along the dorsal border instead of concentrating on the angle, and it does not reach the internal face at all.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.action: Adducts, medially rotates and assists extension of the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula to the crest of the lesser tubercle, next to the latissimus. That adjacency is the point: this record's assessment reads the muscle's scattered distribution — present in turtles, crocodylians and mammals, absent in amphibians and birds — as repeated differentiation out of the latissimus dorsi and subcoracoscapularis field rather than as one ancestral muscle lost three times, and the human arrangement, with the two insertions on adjacent lips of the same groove, is what that hypothesis predicts.

occurrences.name: M. scapulo-humeralis posterior (teres major)
occurrences.innervation: N. scapulo-humeralis, from the N. dorsalis scapulae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer equates his *M. scapulo-humeralis posterior* with the teres major, which is why it is scored here. It follows the scapulo-humeralis profundus, lies dorsal to it, is covered by the dorsalis scapulae, and takes its origin further dorsally on the same bony scapula, inserting on the extensor side of the proximal humerus near the processus medialis. **This record's assessment reads its scattered distribution as repeated differentiation out of the latissimus/subcoracoscapularis field rather than one ancestral muscle**; the tuatara is a lepidosaur that has it, sharing a nerve with the scapulohumeralis in front of it.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. A slight origin from the dorsum of the scapula at its posterior angle and a main origin from the upper two-thirds of the axillary border, where it is bound to the posterior border of the subscapularis by an intermuscular septum giving fibres to both. It receives a slip from the latissimus dorsi and then inserts into the inner lip of the bicipital groove — **separated by a wide interval from the latissimus tendon**, which lands in the floor of the same groove.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. As in the cuscus: scapular angle and the upper two-thirds of the axillary border, a slip received from the latissimus dorsi, insertion into the inner lip of the bicipital groove.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Same origin, different ending: **the teres major and the latissimus dorsi share one insertion here.** A strong tendinous band arches back from the floor of the bicipital groove, twisted on itself so that its posterior border is round and cord-like; the teres major takes the lower half of it, the latissimus the upper, and a few teres fibres reach the humerus directly just below the lesser tubercle. In the cuscus and the phascogale the two insertions are a wide interval apart. The same two muscles, the same two bones, and a shared tendon in one animal where there are two in the others.

homology.notes: Distribution is scattered — present in turtles, crocodylians and mammals, absent in amphibians and birds, uncertain in lepidosaurs. This pattern is more easily read as repeated differentiation from the latissimus dorsi/subcoracoscapularis field than as a single ancestral muscle with three losses.
homology.openQuestion: Is the turtle/crocodylian teres major homologous with the mammalian one, or convergent?

consensus.origin: Thoracolumbar fascia and the neural spines of the posterior thoracic and lumbar vertebrae; in non-mammalian tetrapods, the dorsal fascia over the anterior trunk.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, on or near the crest of the lesser tubercle / deltopectoral region.
consensus.action: Retracts (extends) and adducts the humerus; the principal recovery-stroke muscle in sprawling locomotion.
consensus.innervation: Thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) — dorsal (extensor) division of the brachial plexus.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain, which corrects an earlier note here that claimed a dorsal humeral scar as its insertion. Molnar et al. report no compelling evidence that the latissimus dorsi existed as a muscle separate from the deltoideus in early tetrapodomorph fish; what marks the separation is the appearance of the latissimus dorsi process one node crownward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. The only correlate is a shared one: the thickened posterior margin of the cleithrum above the glenoid, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as the deltoideus plus part of the latissimus dorsi. There is no humeral correlate — the latissimus dorsi process is absent in this taxon and in Gogonasus, and first appears at Elpistostegalia.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The latissimus dorsi attachment is present as a process or a series of diagonal ridges (Vorobyeva 2000; Boisvert 2009; Ahlberg 2011), and its appearance at this node is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the latissimus dorsi from the deltoideus. It sits at the proximal border of the ectepicondyle, which is why they take the muscle to be a derivative of the same superficial dorsal mass rather than a new arrival. In Strepsodus, Rhizodus and Aztecia the reported processes do not resemble these oblique ridges, and Molnar et al. score the latissimus insertion in those taxa as on the dorsal ridge itself.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. One or more ridges on the proximal dorsal humerus (Coates 1996), as in Tiktaalik and Panderichthys rather than the distinct spike of Baphetes and Pederpes; in Ichthyostega the process is probably confluent with the ectepicondyle. No origin is scored — the cleithral scar that would carry it cannot be separated from the deltoideus origin.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: The largest dorsal shoulder muscle, but its origin is entirely fascial — no bony attachment, so no correlate. The insertion is on the posterior face of the same crest that receives the pectoralis and supracoracoideus.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior surface of the crista ventralis of the humerus, by a strong tendon.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Inserts on the lateral face of the deltopectoral crest by a tendon shared with the dorsalis scapulae — see that row. Scoring both on the same landmark is the point rather than a duplication: in salamanders they insert separately.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Retained despite the carapace; origin shifts onto the internal surface of the shell.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin transferred onto the internal surface of the carapace, which is built from the ribs.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.innervation: Thoracodorsal equivalent from the dorsal divisions of the brachial plexus.
occurrences.note: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle is large and its humeral insertion is confluent with that of the teres complex (Kępa et al. 2023).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From an aponeurosis beside the dorsal midline — no bony origin — tendinously onto the proximal dorsal humerus. In Gekko the insertion shifts to the lateral side of the humerus, which is an attachment difference between two geckos and a caution against reading one lizard as Lepidosauria.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. From the thoracodorsal fascia, beginning near the spinous process of the first dorsal vertebra and running linearly back to about the sixth dorsal rib; a large flat tendon passes between triceps longus lateralis and scapulohumeralis brevis to insert on the craniodorsal humerus in common with teres major. **The insertion leaves a large scar about a quarter of the shaft length from the humeral head, as a tubercle or a pit, and it is present even in hatchlings** — an osteological correlate reliable enough to use on a fossil.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Schreiweis (1982) resolves the penguin muscle into cranialis, caudalis and metapatagialis parts.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar. **The insertion is deliberately unrecorded rather than asserted.** This row carried an insertion on the lateral scapula and the clavicle, which is the rhomboideus attachment, not the latissimus: no bird inserts this muscle anywhere but the humerus, and none of the three sources cited here says otherwise. Abdala & Diogo's Tables 1-3 are a synonymy and give no attachment for it; Ghetie et al. (1976) is a plate atlas with no descriptive origin or insertion statements anywhere in its 154 pages; and Schreiweis (1982) describes a penguin, whose latissimus dorsi cranialis inserts on the posterior border of the humeral shaft near the distal border of the pneumatic fossa. Nothing in the corpus states a *Gallus* insertion, so the row now says so instead of guessing. The origin, on the thoracic neural spines, is retained — that much is consistent across every avian source here.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Pars cranialis is the most superficial back muscle, arising aponeurotically over the neural spines of three thoracic vertebrae rather than directly from bone — Matsuoka & Hasegawa say the attachment 'seems not on the bones directly' — and pars caudalis from the neural spines of the posterior thoracics, reaching the dorso-cranial ilium weakly. The two fuse at the armpit and enter the arm through the slit between scapulotriceps and humerotriceps.

**This row previously gave the insertion as the medial scapula and the medial clavicle, which is not what its own source says.** Matsuoka & Hasegawa put the insertion on the linear tuberosity on the caudal surface of the Crista pectoralis of the humerus — the deltopectoral crest under its avian name — immediately beside the much longer attachment of deltoideus major. The medial scapula and clavicle are where they put M. rhomboideus superficialis, one muscle away. The corrected row agrees with this record's own consensus (proximal humerus near the crest of the lesser tubercle), with McKitrick's loon, and with Schreiweis's penguin, whose latissimus ends on the posterior border of the humeral shaft near the pneumatic fossa.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi (pars cranialis + pars caudalis)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. Two separate bellies, 8 mm apart in this specimen. Pars cranialis arises by a short wide aponeurosis from the dorsal vertebrae and inserts by semitendinous fibres on the dorsolateral surface of the humeral shaft, deep to the scapulotriceps. Pars caudalis arises from the dorsal vertebrae cranially and, by aponeurosis, from the medial, cranial and lateral surfaces of the ala preacetabularis ilii — the three ilium rows are that second head, one per aspect McKitrick names, where a single `lateral` row had been standing for all three — and inserts by a 3 mm tendon on the margo caudalis of the humerus, just cranial to the insertion of pars cranialis. A dense tendinous band, George & Berger's 'humeral anchor', ties the tendon to the scapulotriceps.

occurrences.name: Latissimus spinalis + latissimus costalis
occurrences.origin: Spinalis from the neural spines of thoracic vertebrae 2 to 10 or 11 — fleshy to vertebra 7, aponeurotic behind it — plus the external surface of the ventral part of the caudal angle of the scapula and the proximal third of the teres major's aponeurosis of origin; costalis from ribs 8 to 14.
occurrences.insertion: Spinalis by aponeurosis onto a tubercle on the dorsal side of the posterior border of the entepicondylus; costalis by aponeurosis just distal to that, its posterior fibres bypassing the epicondyle to continue into the tensor fasciae antebrachii across a tendinous interseptum.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The latissimus costalis and the tensor fasciae antebrachii form a digastric complex across the elbow, and one of the two specimens lacked the interseptum entirely, the two muscles running continuous as they do in the long-beaked echidna. Gambaryan et al. read the continuous state as primitive and the interseptum as intermediate towards the platypus, where the tensor is a separate muscle — which would make the therian tensor fasciae antebrachii the last remnant of the latissimus costalis.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.action: Extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.innervation: Thoracodorsal equivalent from the dorsal divisions of the brachial plexus.
occurrences.note: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle is large and its humeral insertion is confluent with that of the teres complex (Kępa et al. 2023).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. **Insertion shifted to the lateral surface of the humerus**, against the proximal dorsal surface in Eublepharis. Same bone, different face, and the shift diff reads it as a substantive move on the medial/lateral axis.

occurrences.name: Latissimus spinalis + latissimus costalis
occurrences.origin: Spinalis from the neural spines of thoracic vertebrae 1 or 2 to 11 or 12 — fleshy to the fifth or sixth and aponeurotic behind that — plus slips from ribs 7 and 8 and a slip from the external surface of the ventral part of the caudal angle of the scapula; costalis as slips from five to seven ribs beginning at rib 8.
occurrences.insertion: Spinalis by aponeurosis onto a distinct tubercle on the dorsal side of the posterior border of the entepicondylus of the humerus; costalis by a first aponeurosis just distal to it, then continuing as the fascia antebrachii.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The insertion is the finding, and it is at the wrong end of the bone: in therians and in extant reptiles the latissimus ends near the lesser tubercle, and here it ends on the medial epicondyle. Gambaryan et al. read it as secondary and tie it to the barrel-shaped monotreme rib cage — the elbow falls in the same parasagittal plane as the widest point of the ribs, so the muscle runs straight down the flank onto the epicondyle.

parts.name: Latissimus costalis
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. state that a latissimus costalis of this kind — rib-borne, alongside a separate spinal head — is found nowhere outside monotremes.

occurrences.name: Latissimus spinalis + latissimus costalis
occurrences.origin: Spinalis from the neural spines of thoracic vertebrae 3 to 11, fleshy to vertebra 7 and aponeurotic behind it, with no scapular or costal slip; costalis from ribs 8 to 15.
occurrences.insertion: Spinalis mainly fleshy along the postaxial aspect of the humerus, from the distal angle of the pectoral crest to the entepicondylar foramen, leaving a distinct facet; costalis by a flat tendon along the posterior side of the pectoral crest, PROXIMAL to the spinalis rather than distal to it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The order of the two insertions is reversed against both echidnas — costalis proximal and spinalis distal here, the other way round in Tachyglossidae — and the spinalis insertion has climbed back up the humerus from the epicondyle towards the pectoral crest. That proximal shift is what crowds the coracobrachialis longus distally in this animal.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.action: Retracts and adducts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tawa hallae, Burch (2014), extant-phylogenetic-bracket reconstruction. **Insertion is a Level I inference with a real correlate**: the scar on the lateral humerus posterior to the deltopectoral crest is present in crocodylians, birds AND lepidosaurs, and may be a rugose tubercle, a crest, a pit or a linear sulcus. The origin is weaker — the exact extent in theropods is equivocal, so Burch reconstructs it only as arising from the thoracodorsal fascia in the region of the first to fifth dorsal vertebrae, and no vertebral row is asserted here. Reconstructed as a single muscle: birds divide it in two, but the parts are variably present across the clade and sometimes form a continuous sheet.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.action: Extends and medially rotates the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Vertebral spines from T7 to the sacrum, the posterior third of the iliac crest, the lower three or four ribs and sometimes the inferior angle of the scapula, to the floor of the intertubercular groove. **The scapular slip is scored because Gest scores it as variable**, and it is the interesting one — a muscle of the body wall picking up an attachment on the girdle bone it passes. The origin has spread much further caudally than in any outgroup here; the insertion has not moved, which is the pattern this record shows throughout.

occurrences.name: M. latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). A narrow aponeurotic band from the dorsal aspect of the neural spines of the posteriormost cervical and the first seven thoracic vertebrae, continuous across the midline with its fellow and filling the spaces between adjacent spines. It tapers markedly, passes **between the scapular and coracoid heads of the triceps**, and attaches to the dorsal aspect of the proximal humerus, the posterior fibres folding deep to the anterior ones to insert more proximally. Compare the avian rows on this record, where the insertion was for a time written onto the scapula and clavicle; the lizard shows the plesiomorphic arrangement plainly.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Flat and large, its fibres running obliquely forward, from the thoracodorsal fascia along the vertebral spinous processes in the midline and, ventrocaudally, from the dorsal margins of the first five ribs. Insertion on the caudal surface of the proximal humerus. **The costal origin is the difference from Russell & Bauer**, who give the neural spines of the last cervical and first seven thoracic vertebrae and no rib at all; Freitas et al. present the extension onto ribs as the *Varanus* condition after Jenkins & Goslow (1983) and report it here as well. Dorsally the muscle is continuous with the trapezius.

occurrences.name: M. latissimus dorsi (dorso-humeralis)
occurrences.innervation: N. latissimus dorsi, from the N. brachialis longus superior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. From the spinous processes of the fifth to seventeenth vertebrae to the posterior surface of the proximal humerus, below the insertion of the scapulo-humeralis profundus. Humerus, as in every other column on this record — see the *Gallus* and *Cygnus* rows, where a scapula-and-clavicle insertion had been asserted and was removed.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The origin is the same in all three: the spines of every thoracic vertebra except the first two, the lumbar aponeurosis, and a single digitation from the last rib. **It overlaps the posterior angle of the scapula and in no case takes any fibres from it** — worth setting against the human row on this record, where Gest scores an occasional slip from the inferior angle. Near its insertion the muscle divides: the upper, smaller slip passes behind the other and joins the posterior margin of the teres major to be inserted with it, while the main posterior portion gives off the dorsi-epitrochlear and then ends in a flat shining tendon that runs out under both heads of the biceps into the floor of the broad shallow bicipital groove, abutting the pectoralis major.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The origin is the same in all three: the spines of every thoracic vertebra except the first two, the lumbar aponeurosis, and a single digitation from the last rib. **It overlaps the posterior angle of the scapula and in no case takes any fibres from it** — worth setting against the human row on this record, where Gest scores an occasional slip from the inferior angle. The insertion is identical to the cuscus's — a slip to the teres major, the dorsi-epitrochlear given off, and the main tendon into the floor of the bicipital groove. The dorsi-epitrochlear is relatively best developed in this animal of the three.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The origin is the same in all three: the spines of every thoracic vertebra except the first two, the lumbar aponeurosis, and a single digitation from the last rib. **It overlaps the posterior angle of the scapula and in no case takes any fibres from it** — worth setting against the human row on this record, where Gest scores an occasional slip from the inferior angle. **The insertion is shared with the teres major** through the twisted tendinous arch described on that record: the latissimus takes its upper part, the teres major the lower. The dorsi-epitrochlear is still given off, but instead of reaching the olecranon on its own it joins the triceps near the elbow and is inserted with it.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. latissimus dorsi.** The anterior part arises by a thin aponeurosis 7 centimeters wide from the neural crests of the thoracic vertebrae. This origin (figs. 18, 22) is just superficial to the origin of M. rhomb. superf. Another apo- neurosis, starting approximately |] centimeter posterior to the anterior one and going caudad to the fascial origin of M. extens. ilio-tib. ant., forms the origin for the posterior band of M. lat. dorsi. There may also be fascial origin from the connective tissue overlying the costal musculature. In some instances the origin of the posterior band is deep to the origin of the dermal part, but this seems to be less frequent in occurrence than is the formation of the dermal component as *Insertion.* The anterior part inserts fleshily on a narrow line, some 5 centimeters long, beginning about four centimeters from the proximal end of the humerus. The belly enters the musculature of the upper arm MUSCLES OF THE WING 49 palmar to the scapular head of M. triceps and anconal to the entrance of M. lat. dorsi, post. pt. The tendon of this latter part of the muscle attaches to the deep side of the anterior part but also inserts on the humerus beneath the fleshy insertion of the anterior portion.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial).

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pipa pipa, Prikryl et al. (2009). **Runs from the humerus to the pelvis.** It originates on the humerus and passes back along the flanks to insert on the posterior part of the lateral surface of the iliac shaft and on the dorsal fascia. Compare *Xenopus*, where the same muscle ends on two thigh muscles instead — the two pipids both extend it far past the shoulder, by different routes.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Xenopus laevis, Prikryl et al. (2009). **A peculiar feature of this animal, and the reason a pelvic-and-thigh paper describes a forelimb muscle**: it covers the suprascapula and runs back as far as the glutaeus maximus and cruralis, fusing with their superficial layers, so a shoulder muscle ends on two thigh muscles. Superficial, also attached to a dorsal fascia. Its function remains rotation of the forelimb backwards despite the posterior extent. **Neither end is bone.** The origin on the dorsal fascia is scored on `dorsal-fascia-anuran`; the insertion is onto the superficial layers of the glutaeus maximus and cruralis, which are both this dataset's `extensor-iliotibialis`, so the row carries it as `muscle: extensor-iliotibialis`. A shoulder muscle ending on two thigh muscles is the observation, and it is now recorded as an attachment rather than described in prose beside an empty field.

homology.notes: Unbroken across every taxon sampled and one of the few muscles whose insertion is reliably identifiable on fossil humeri. Its dorsal-mass derivation and thoracodorsal innervation are constant.
homology.teaching: Best single muscle for demonstrating that a large axio-appendicular muscle can survive a radical girdle rebuild (turtle shell, bird flight apparatus) without losing identity.

consensus.origin: Scapula near the glenoid (scapular head) plus one or more humeral heads along the shaft.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon process of the ulna.
consensus.action: Extends the elbow; the scapular head also retracts the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve (C6–T1) — the defining nerve of the dorsal/extensor mass.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.note: Eusthenopteron foordi. Scored uncertain, and the earlier note here — 'inferred from the olecranon and from humeral shaft rugosities' — is wrong on this source's own evidence. Tetrapodomorph-fish ulnae lack an ossified olecranon; the olecranon and the posterior ulnar crest appear together at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, and their appearance is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the triceps from the extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris. Here the superficial dorsal musculature probably inserted on the proximal ulna without leaving a mark (Andrews & Westoll 1970a). Molnar et al. call it tempting to homologise the dorsal process of the Latimeria ulna with the olecranon, and decline.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. An ossified olecranon process with a confluent posterior crest, present in every stem tetrapod here whose ulna is preserved — Ichthyostega, where it is bifurcated and extremely well developed, Tulerpeton and Pederpes as well. Crassigyrinus is the exception: its presumed ulna appears to have neither feature. No origin is scored; the triceps leaves no correlate on the girdle in Iguana, and none is traced here.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (anconaeus group)
occurrences.note: Multi-headed in urodeles, with scapular and several humeral heads.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Four separately named heads, two girdle and two humeral, converging on one olecranon insertion. The coracoid and scapular heads unite about midway along the humerus. This is the clearest case in the dataset of a muscle whose head count is a naming decision: Mivart (1869) and Davison (1895) called the whole complex 'triceps', Francis (1934) named all four.
occurrences.origin: Four heads: coracoid (anconaeus coracoideus, by a long tendon); scapula posterior to the glenoid and the joint capsule (anconaeus scapularis medialis); proximal two-thirds of the lateral face of the humerus (anconaeus humeralis lateralis); the whole posterior face of the humerus (anconaeus humeralis medialis).
occurrences.insertion: Olecranon process of the ulna.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.action: In anurans, a major decelerator during landing rather than a propulsive extensor.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.divisionNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. THREE heads, where salamanders have a fourth point of origin at the coracoid (Francis 1934). A head lost, and one of the few places in this dataset where a division count differs between two amphibian orders by a stated absence rather than by a difference in how authors carve the muscle up.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Origins on the humerus (caput mediale and laterale) and the scapula (caput scapulare). No insertion row: Sigurdsen et al. say the muscle extends the elbow and is well defined in both anurans and salamanders but do not state where it ends, and the anuran zeugopodium is a fused radio-ulna, so inheriting the consensus olecranon would assert a landmark on a bone this taxon does not have as such.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Two heads. The smaller scapular head arises by a narrow tendon onto the scapula just dorsal to the glenoid, and in *Pseudemys* that tendon **perforates the latissimus dorsi-teres major tendon** — the two rows on this animal are physically threaded through one another. The humeral head takes most of the dorsal humeral shaft. They converge on a common tendon over the elbow onto the olecranon and the adjacent posterior border of the ulna. Primarily an antebrachial flexor, but the scapular head also crosses the shoulder.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Insertion scars on the olecranon process.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.note: Attachments are deliberately not scored for Alligator mississippiensis. Allen et al. measure architecture without attachment sites, and Abdala & Diogo's crocodylian is Caiman latirostris. The rows this occurrence used to carry were Klinkhamer et al.'s Crocodylus porosus description and have moved. Worth acquiring a source for: the triceps longus medialis of Alligator is reported with TWO tendons of origin, one scapular and one CORACOID, and that second head is the character Klinkhamer et al.'s Crocodylus finding is measured against — see the Crocodylus porosus occurrence.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus, and this row carries the ONLY forelimb difference Klinkhamer et al. found between it and other crocodilians. Triceps longus medialis arises by a single tendon from the postero-lateral and proximal scapula; in Alligator mississippiensis and other crocodilian taxa the same muscle is reported with two tendons of origin, one scapular and one from the CORACOID, and only the scapular tendon was found here. So the absent coracoid head is the point of the row, and no coracoid origin is scored. Triceps longus lateralis also arises by tendon from the proximo-lateral scapula, superficial to teres major and scapulohumeralis caudalis but deep to deltoideus scapularis. Triceps brevis is three-part: TB1 fleshy on the proximo-lateral humerus over the teres major insertion, TB2 on the postero-dorsal and proximal humerus, TB3 on the posterior humeral head. All heads converge by tendon on the olecranon.

occurrences.name: Scapulotriceps + humerotriceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. TWO INSERTION ROWS, because McKitrick gives the two heads two different sites. Scapulotriceps arises semitendinously from the dorsal surface of the head of the scapula and from the ligament between the scapular head and the fossa pneumotricipitalis of the humerus; its tendon runs over the sulcus m. scapulotricipitis to insert on the PROCESSUS COTYLARIS DORSALIS — which is not the olecranon, so that row stops at the bone rather than manufacturing a correlate. Humerotriceps arises from the ventral and dorsal fossae pneumotricipitales, the tuberculum dorsale, and most of the length of the caudal surface of the humerus, and inserts on the OLECRANON, which McKitrick names plainly and which skeleton.json carries as a correlate — so it is scored. Both heads had been collapsed onto one landmark-free row, and the reasoning that justified that for the scapulotriceps was suppressing a site the source states for the humerotriceps. McKitrick records a disagreement worth keeping — there is NO 'furcular' origin of the scapulotriceps in loons, against Sanders (1967). In Gavia stellata the two tendons of insertion are separate but connected by fascia, against Sanders (1967) again.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, medial heads)
occurrences.action: Extends the forearm; the long head also extends and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Six well-separated bellies near the origin in this animal — caput longum, laterale, angulare, accessorium, mediale accessorium and mediale, the last itself three-bellied.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (five heads)
occurrences.origin: Both long heads by a superficial aponeurosis from a crest running down the middle of the lower part of the external surface of the scapula to the glenoid, the profundus curving further caudal to the glenoid and close to the coracoid; lateralis by a narrow tendon a little proximal to the centre of the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus; medialis and accessorius from the proximal and distal dorsal surfaces of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Longus superficialis on the posterior projection of the olecranon apex, over more than half its extent; longus profundus across almost the whole apex from posterior to anterior projection; lateralis on the anterior projection; accessorius along the apical border of the humerus-facing aspect and medialis on the surface between that border and the elbow joint facet.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Five heads, and the two scapular ones are the point: the superficialis arises cranial to the profundus and inserts posterior to it, so the two pull the ulna criss-cross. Gambaryan et al. suggest that suits the ball-and-socket monotreme elbow, which among tetrapods is otherwise an anuran arrangement.
occurrences.divisionNote: A divided triceps longus is listed among the ADVANCED monotreme features, against the primitive ones. Gambaryan et al. note that mustelids carry a second two-jointed scapular head, the caput angulare (Ercoli et al. 2015), which resembles the monotreme triceps longus superficialis; if those are homologous the double-headed scapular triceps is primitive for mammals as a whole. The Galictis row on this record is from the companion paper.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (five heads)
occurrences.origin: Both long heads by a superficial aponeurosis from a crest on the lower part of the external surface of the scapula running to the glenoid; lateralis fleshy from the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus just distal to the shoulder joint capsule; medialis and accessorius united at their origin on the dorsal surface of the humerus and separated further distally by a neurovascular bundle.
occurrences.insertion: Longus superficialis on the posterior projection of the olecranon apex, over about a quarter of its extent; longus profundus across almost the whole apex; lateralis on the anterior projection; accessorius and medialis on the humerus-facing aspect, aided by aponeuroses posteriorly and anteriorly respectively.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The triceps lateralis is separated from the other four heads by a neurovascular bundle in every genus, which is what makes the accessorius readable as a proximal subdivision of the medialis rather than an independent head.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (five heads)
occurrences.origin: Both long heads from the scapular crest running to the glenoid; lateralis by a narrow tendon from a distinct tubercle on the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, between the infraspinatus insertion and the brachialis origin; medialis and accessorius from the dorsal surface of the humerus, their origins completely separate from one another.
occurrences.insertion: Longus superficialis on the posterior projection of the olecranon apex over about a quarter of its extent; longus profundus across almost the whole apex; lateralis fleshy on the anterior projection, nearly fusing behind with the accessorius; accessorius and medialis on the humerus-facing aspect.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The lateralis origin has a named bony tubercle here where the echidnas have only a surface, and the medialis and accessorius origins are fully separate where in Tachyglossidae they are united.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.action: Principal extensor of the antebrachium; contributes to humeral extension.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **The muscle is unambiguous; the number of heads is not.** Birds and crocodylians share the scapular and medial heads, birds have reduced the coracoid head to a vestige and lost the lateral head entirely. Three heads are scored here and the coracoid head is not — it may already have been vestigial or absent in basal theropods, on the chameleon parallel where its loss goes with increased humeral mobility (Jasinoski et al. 2006).

Caput scapulare: a small tendinous area just posterodorsal to the scapular lip of the glenoid, lightly striated in *Tawa* though without the distinct tubercle other theropods develop. Caput mediale: a wide fleshy origin over the posteromedial humeral shaft, bifid proximally around the scapulohumeralis insertion, with no scars anywhere in theropods. **Caput laterale is the contested head** — Jasinoski et al. (2006) declined to reconstruct it in dromaeosaurids for want of the crocodylian lateral triceps ridge, but Burch identifies a ridge in that position in many theropods including *Tawa*, the same one bounding the deltoideus clavicularis insertion posteriorly, and reads it as this head's linear origin. All three converge on one tendon; the *Tawa* olecranon is short but carries faint striations on its posterior surface.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.action: Extends the forearm; the long head extends and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Three heads: long from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, lateral from the posterolateral humerus and lateral intermuscular septum, medial from the posteromedial surface of the lower half of the humerus, all onto the olecranon. **Three heads is not the ancestral count.** Crocodylians and lepidosaurs have four — scapular, coracoid, medial and lateral — and Burch reconstructs three in *Tawa* with the coracoid head already lost. Birds have lost the lateral head as well. The human long head is the scapular head; the coracoid head is gone with the coracoid, which is the same absence the subcoracoscapularis row records. The infraglenoid tubercle is scored as `scapula` without a landmark, since it is a named point on that bone rather than an element here.

occurrences.name: M. triceps brachii (scapulotriceps + humerotriceps)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). **Two muscles, not three heads, and the coracoid head is gone.** Scapulotriceps has a dorsal head from the posterior tip of the dorsal surface of the furcula and a deeper one from the posterior half of the dorsal lip of the coracoid-scapular glenoid, together with Lig. coracohumerale dorsale, plus a small flat branching tendon — the humeral anchor — from the proximal base of the Crista pectoralis on the caudal humerus. Its distal half is tendinous and inserts on the dorso-caudal lip of the proximal ulna, running in the Sulcus m. scapulotricipitis. Humerotriceps is Y-shaped: the dorsal belly attaches along the entire ventro-caudal surface of the humeral shaft, leaving an especially deep impression, and the ventral head arises from the roof and internal groove inside the Fossa pneumotricipitalis, its tendon running like a bowstring to the olecranon. Compare *Tawa*, where Burch reconstructs three heads with the coracoid head already lost; birds have since lost the lateral head as well.

occurrences.name: M. triceps complex
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Four heads, and only two of them reach the girdle.** The scapular head arises from the dorsal glenoid buttress with its fibres bound into the Y-shaped scapulohumeral ligament complex; the coracoid head arises not from the coracoid at all but from a long ligamentous band forming part of the sternoscapular ligament, and the two together form a loop around the latissimus dorsi insertion. The lateral humeral head arises from a concavity dorsal to the deltopectoral crest and from much of the anterodorsal shaft; the medial from a concavity on the dorsal proximal humerus, its ventral limit set by the coracobrachialis insertions. Distally the two humeral heads enclose the dorsal border of the shaft for its distal half. All four interweave into one motor tendon onto the olecranon, with the **patella ulnaris** embedded in the humeral heads' common tendon. Compare *Tawa*, where Burch reconstructs three heads with the coracoid head already lost, and birds, which have lost the lateral head too.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Fusiform, its fibres running along the lateral surface of the humerus, from the dorsal aspect of the deltopectoral crest to the olecranon. **Freitas et al. use Meers's (2003) crocodilian names for the four heads rather than the lizard ones**, on the ground that this animal's triceps resembles the crocodilian arrangement more closely; that is why the four heads appear here under names that do not match Russell & Bauer's scapular, coracoid, lateral humeral and medial humeral heads for the same animal. They also argue in passing that the group may not be a triceps at all, and that settling it would need ontogeny and innervation rather than topography.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). **The paper's headline observation.** This head arises by a tendinous arc on the lateral surface of the shoulder, spanning from the scapula to the dorsal surface of the deltopectoral crest, its thin tendon broadening where it meets the bone and the arc itself overlying the coracobrachialis brevis laterally. A tendinous arc origin for the long caudal head had been described only in crocodilians, where it spans scapula to coracoid (Meers 2003; Romão et al. 2016); Freitas et al. report it in a lizard for the first time and note that the second attachment is the deltopectoral crest rather than the coracoid. Romão et al. read the crocodilian arc as related to aquatic habits, which an iguana does not share, and Freitas et al. leave the question open rather than claiming convergence.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). From the medial surface of the proximal humerus to the olecranon, with a second tendon that Freitas et al. describe as arising medially on the sternum — an unusual attachment for a triceps head, and one they record without comment. It is scored because the table states it plainly and at both ends; a reader should know that no other source here gives this muscle a girdle origin, and that Russell & Bauer's medial humeral head in the same animal arises from a concavity on the dorsal proximal humerus with its ventral limit set by the coracobrachialis insertions, and reaches no further.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Long and narrow, from the craniodorsal surface of the humerus to the olecranon. In *V. exanthematicus* the corresponding lateral head takes an additional origin from an aponeurosis shared with the brachialis (Jenkins & Goslow 1983); Freitas et al. record only the humeral origin here. All four heads reach the olecranon through a common tendon.

occurrences.name: M. anconaeus
occurrences.innervation: Rr. anconaei of the N. radialis superficialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther called it *M. triceps*; Osawa counts **four heads**. Caput scapulare by a slender tendon from the scapulohumeral ligament and from the scapula dorsal to the glenoid, between the origins of the scapulo-humeralis profundus and posterior; caput coracoideum by a very thin tendon from a point at the caudal angle of the inner surface of the coracoid; caput humerale laterale from the lateral side of the whole humeral shaft; caput humerale mediale from the medial side below the processus medialis as far as the elbow capsule. All insert on the posterior elbow capsule, the olecranon and the proximal ulna, and Osawa separates the capsular part as a *M. subanconaeus*.

**Four heads is the full count**, and it is what the archosaur columns are measured against: Burch reconstructs three for *Tawa* with the coracoid head already lost, birds have lost the lateral head as well, and the human long head is the scapular head with the coracoid one gone with the bone.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.innervation: Musculo-spiral nerve, which pierces and divides the internal head.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus, in which Cunningham thought the triceps reaches its maximum development. The scapular head has **two sets of fibres, not one**: a tendinous origin from the bone beside the glenoid, giving the long head as usually seen, and above that a series of short fleshy fasciculi off the scapular border that curve down as a thin layer and blend into the long head's upper third — so the long head runs along nearly the whole axillary border. The external head takes the upper half of the humerus posteriorly and is blended there with the brachialis anticus through the external intermuscular septum. **The internal head runs the entire length of the humerus and is pierced and split in two by the musculo-spiral nerve**; in the other two animals it is weak, stops at the teres major insertion, and is not pierced. The three heads stay separate until the olecranon. Cunningham contradicts Macalister here, who had written that in marsupials the lateral heads are fused into one inseparable humeral muscle: 'I did not find this to be the case.'

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Three separable heads, differing from the thylacine's in three ways Cunningham lists: the long head comes off no more than a third of the scapular border and all from one tendon; the internal head is weak and does not reach above the teres major insertion, and **is not pierced by the musculo-spiral nerve**; and the three heads blend higher up the limb. Cunningham's summary is that this triceps closely resembles a human one.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Three separable heads, differing from the thylacine's in three ways Cunningham lists: the long head comes off no more than a third of the scapular border and all from one tendon; the internal head is weak and does not reach above the teres major insertion, and **is not pierced by the musculo-spiral nerve**; and the three heads blend higher up the limb. Cunningham's summary is that this triceps closely resembles a human one.

occurrences.name: Scapulotriceps + humerotriceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026). Rows are the **scapulotriceps**: a tendinous origin on the proximal scapula immediately caudal to the glenoid, where a circular rugose tubercle marks it, inserting on the proximal caudal humeral shaft. **The insertion leaves two correlates** — a long lateral scar and a smaller circular scar proximal to it. On dissection of the scanned specimen the belly of pars caudalis lies ventral to pars cranialis and thins until it is indistinguishable from it near the insertion. **M. humerotriceps.** This muscle covers much of the caudal surface of the humerus. The origin is fleshy on the caudal humeral head, extending into the pneumatic fossa. The origin is slightly bifurcated by the crus dorsale. In many birds, the proximal area of origin of this muscle is clearly marked by intermuscular lines. We observed these intermuscular lines in a variety of bird genera within the collections of the NMNH, but none could be found for Chauna. The belly of the muscle contacts the humeral shaft for nearly all of its length. It becomes tendinous distally, and inserts on the olecranon of the ulna. **M. scapulotriceps.** The tendinous origin of M. scapulotriceps is on the proximal scapula immediately caudal to the glenoid, where a circular rugose tubercle can be found. The muscle im- The origin is on the lateral head of the coracoid via a sheetlike tendon, ventral to the origin of M. coracobrachialis cranialis, and extends onto the bicipital crest and dorsally up the ventral portion of the cranial face of the proximal humerus. A clear facet on the lateral coracoid head is associated with this muscle’s origin. As it approaches the distal head of the humerus, the muscle becomes tendinous. This tendon then splits in two, inserting onto the bicipital tubercles of the radius and ulna.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. triceps.** The origin of the scapular head of M. triceps is from a dorso- ventral line 1.5 centimeters wide which lies on the posterior edge of the head of the scapula and just posterior to the origin of M. delt. major. This is a mixed fleshy and tendinous origin. There is also strong fascial origin from the anterior edge of the proximal part of M. dorsalis scap. The external head arises fleshily from the posterior half of the anconal surface of the humerus from the proximal part of the bicipital surface distad to the beginning of the distal third of the humeral length. This includes part of the origin of the internal head, the rest of which has previously been described. Insertion—The strong, ba *Insertion.* The strong, band-like tendon formed at the level of the humeral condyles contributes to, or at least is attached to, the joint mem- brane but continues distally to insert on the anconal surface of the ulna MUSCLES OF THE WING 59 in an obliquely antero-posterior line some 3 centimeters long and 1.5 centimeters from the proximal end of the ulna (fig. 18).

homology.notes: Present in every tetrapod examined. The number of heads varies freely (three in mammals, more in urodeles and crocodylians) without disturbing the identity of the complex — a useful reminder that head count is not a homology criterion.
homology.teaching: The canonical dorsal-mass muscle: origin on the girdle and humerus, insertion on the ulna, radial innervation, elbow extension. Every other extensor can be introduced by reference to it.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.
