muscles.name: Brachialis / humeroantebrachialis
synonyms: brachialis inferior (Romer 1944; Walker 1973; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Anterior surface of the humeral shaft, distal to the deltopectoral crest.
consensus.insertion: Proximal ulna (and radius in some taxa).
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow. Because it crosses only the elbow, it is the pure elbow flexor regardless of forearm position.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6) — ventral division.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The ventral median ridge of the radius, which usually carries obvious muscle scars and is read as the humeroantebrachialis insertion (Bishop 2014). Two statements in Molnar et al. sit awkwardly together: they list this ridge among the four longitudinal ridges of the radius in this taxon and label it in their Fig. 10F, yet their character mapping puts the ridge's first appearance at the last common ancestor of crown tetrapods, where it marks the separation of this muscle from the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The row follows the description of the bone. No origin is scored — the ventromedial deltopectoral crest scars that carry it in Baphetes, Crassigyrinus and Ossinodus are not reported here.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Origin from scars on the ventromedial aspect of the deltopectoral crest (Bishop 2014) — the same region Milner & Lindsay (1998) read as the humeroantebrachialis ('brachialis') origin in Baphetes and Smithson (1985) in Crassigyrinus; insertion on the ventral median ridge of the radius. In Necturus and Iguana the origin likewise includes part of the deltopectoral crest, which is the extant end of the same arrangement.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.note: In urodeles the brachialis field is not separated from the biceps field; the single muscle is called humeroantebrachialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thick and parallel-fibred, crossing only the elbow. It has no girdle head, which is the difference from the amniote biceps brachii and the reason the two are not interchangeable.
occurrences.origin: Anterior surface of the proximal humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal end of the radius.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Walker's M. brachialis inferior. Arises from and covers most of the flexor surface of the humeral shaft; fibres run diagonally between the forearm extensors and flexors to a short broad tendon on the ventral surface of the proximal third of the ulna and the adjacent radius. The origin's extent varies: proximally to the coracobrachialis brevis insertion in trionychids, restricted to the distal half of the humerus in testudinines and sea turtles.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the lateral and ventral humeral shaft to the proximal radius and ulna. In Gekko the origin is confined to the lateral shaft.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy on the anterior humeral head; inserts on the proximomedial radius with the biceps tendon.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A rectangular muscle, fleshy at both ends: from the fossa m. brachialis of the humerus to the cranioventral surface of the proximal ulna, in the depressio m. brachialis. Both are named depressions, and both are as close to a clean osteological correlate as this forelimb gets. As in Gavia stellata and Pelecanoides garnoti.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the elbow.
occurrences.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve, with a variable radial contribution.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From a wide area of the lateral surface and craniodistal humeral diaphysis onto the medial ulna and the radius.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Origin **confined to the lateral humeral shaft**; in Eublepharis it takes the ventral surface as well.

occurrences.name: Brachialis ulnaris + brachialis radialis
occurrences.origin: Radialis wedging proximally onto the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus between the triceps lateralis in front and the triceps accessorius behind, then descending along the anterior dorsoventral line; ulnaris anterior and distal to it, reaching a little onto the distal ventral surface around the preaxial side of the bone.
occurrences.insertion: Ulnaris on the radial edge of the posterior surface of the ulna just distal to the elbow joint; radialis just distal to that on the posterior surface of the radius, descending almost to its midlength.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Romer (1922) held the origin on the distal ventral surface of the humerus to be the primitive tetrapod condition and its spread onto the proximal dorsal surface to be a synapsid advance; this genus keeps a trace of the ventral origin that the other two have lost. Allen (1912) mistook the radial head for the brachioradialis.
occurrences.divisionNote: Gambaryan et al. read the two-headed brachialis as a remnant of a stage with freer rotation of the radius against the ulna, since intra-antebrachial mobility in living monotremes is extremely reduced — a muscle keeping a division its joint no longer uses.

occurrences.name: Brachialis ulnaris + brachialis radialis
occurrences.origin: Both heads side by side on the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, the ulnaris anterior to the radialis, the radialis approaching the humeral head anterior to the triceps lateralis origin.
occurrences.insertion: Ulnaris on the radial edge of the posterior surface of the ulna just distal to the elbow joint; radialis just distal to it on the posterior surface of the radius, descending almost to its midlength.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The two heads are furthest apart in this genus and closest together in the platypus, with the long-beaked echidna between them.

occurrences.name: Brachialis ulnaris + brachialis radialis
occurrences.origin: The two heads least separate of the three genera, arising together from the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus and widely separating the triceps lateralis origin in front from the triceps accessorius behind.
occurrences.insertion: As in the echidnas, but the radialis insertion on the radius is shorter; the ulna carries a groove for the flat terminal tendon of the ulnaris.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The groove on the ulna is an osteological correlate for a tendon, which is rarer in this dataset than a scar for a fleshy attachment.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the forearm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **An absent feature is the evidence here.** In all birds the origin is the Fossa musculus brachialis, an impression on the cranial surface of the distal humerus just proximal to the condyles; in crocodylians, lepidosaurs and turtles it is an elongate origin from the distal deltopectoral crest running along much of the anterolateral shaft. The anterior intercondylar depression of many theropods may record the avian distal migration, but it is absent or poorly developed in *Tawa* and *Herrerasaurus*, so the proximal origin is retained. Langer et al. (2007) read that depression the other way and reconstruct a distal origin; Burch notes the proximal placement also gives the longer moment arm. Insertion in common with biceps on the proximal radius and ulna as in crocodylians, rather than restricted to the ulna as in birds — there is no anterior ulnar depression (Impressio brachialis) in theropods to indicate otherwise.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the forearm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior surface of the lower half of the humerus and the intermuscular septa, to the coronoid process of the ulna. Ulna only — the shared radius-and-ulna insertion of crocodylians and lepidosaurs, which Burch reconstructs for *Tawa*, has been restricted to the ulna in humans as it has independently in birds. Two clades arriving at the same restriction is the reason the *Tawa* row scores the plesiomorphic pattern on the absence of an anterior ulnar depression rather than on parsimony alone.

occurrences.name: M. brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only: a thick short muscle from the Fossa m. brachialis on the cranial surface of the distal humerus. The insertion lies beyond this paper, which is Part 1 and covers the muscles attaching to the sternum, coracoid, clavicle, scapula and humerus. **The fossa itself is the point of comparison**: Burch (2014) uses its absence in *Tawa* and *Herrerasaurus* as the evidence that basal theropods retained the proximal, crocodylian-style origin, because in birds this muscle has migrated distally into exactly this impression.

occurrences.name: M. brachialis anticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Fleshy origin from the distal aspect of the deltopectoral crest and the anterior margin of the humeral shaft for its entire length, with some fibres from the intermuscular septum against the lateral triceps head. Its origin is defined by what surrounds it — Russell & Bauer delimit it by the confluence of the deltoid, supracoracoideus and pectoralis insertions above and the biceps and triceps borders either side. **The insertion is in two parts and both muscles contribute to both**: an enlarged part of the common tendon crosses the elbow dorsal to the main brachialis tendon and inserts on the proximomedial radial shaft chiefly by brachialis fibres, while a shorter tendon contributed equally by biceps and brachialis passes behind the radius to the proximal anterior ulna. This is the elongate proximal origin Burch reconstructs for *Tawa* against the distal, avian one.

occurrences.name: M. humero-antibrachialis medialis
occurrences.innervation: N. humero-antibrachialis, from the N. musculo-cutaneus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *humero-antibrachialis inferior*, Günther's *M. brachialis internus* — and this record already carries `humeroantebrachialis` as the amphibian synonym. From almost the entire flexor surface of the humerus as far as the elbow, inserting together with the biceps tendon on the proximal radius and ulna, with a number of fibres going to the elbow capsule. The shared insertion with the biceps is the plesiomorphic condition Burch reconstructs for *Tawa* and that birds and humans have each restricted independently.

occurrences.name: Brachialis anticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **A linear origin from the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft**, under cover of the external head of the triceps and separated from it by a well-marked external intermuscular septum — not the anterior surface a human brachialis comes off. The muscle then winds round the bone, clothing its outer surface, to reach the front of the limb at the elbow and insert behind the gleno-ulnar head of the biceps on the coronoid process.

occurrences.name: Brachialis anticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. As in the thylacine, and differing in taking fibres from the outer aspect of the humeral shaft as well as the posterior, and in a closer connection with the external intermuscular septum. The spiral course round the bone is the same.

occurrences.name: Brachialis anticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. As in the thylacine, and differing in taking fibres from the outer aspect of the humeral shaft as well as the posterior, and in a closer connection with the external intermuscular septum. The spiral course round the bone is the same.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. brachialis.** The origin of this muscle is in the deeply excavated brachial fossa of the distal cranial humerus. It stretches across the elbow joint to insert on the brachial impression of the proximal ventral ulna, deep to the insertion of M. entepicondyloulnaris.

homology.notes: The amphibian humeroantebrachialis and the amniote brachialis occupy the same field. Note the naming hazard: 'humeroantebrachialis' is used by Diogo & Abdala (2007) for the lepidosaur BICEPS, not the brachialis. Always check which sense an author intends.
homology.teaching: A terminology trap worth setting deliberately: the same name denotes different muscles in the urodele and lepidosaur literature.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Biceps brachii / coracoradialis
synonyms: short and long heads of biceps brachii (Jouffroy 1971)

consensus.origin: Coracoid or scapula near the glenoid — the muscle spans the shoulder as well as the elbow.
consensus.insertion: Radius (radial tuberosity), and via the bicipital aponeurosis to the antebrachial fascia in mammals.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm; weak shoulder flexion.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6) — ventral division.

occurrences.note: Absent in Ambystoma ordinarium, but a coracoradialis is present in other urodeles.

occurrences.name: Coracoradialis
occurrences.note: The anuran name records the coracoid origin and radial insertion directly.

occurrences.name: Coracoradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Xenopus laevis. A long tendon runs from the coracoradialis to the radio-ulna, and in this species it is housed: a partially covered groove runs from the deltopectoral crest along part of the ventral surface of the humeral shaft to accommodate it, immediately lateral to a prominent boss for the pectoralis insertion. Ritland (1955a) reports a similar groove in Alytes. The insertion is scored on the radius, which is the element the dataset has for the fused radio-ulna; the groove is a correlate of the TENDON'S PATH rather than of an attachment, which is why no row is put on the humerus.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii

parts.name: Biceps superficialis
parts.note: Two-bellied. The medial belly from the posterior border of the medial half of the coracoid to a tendon at the level of the intertubercular fossa; the lateral belly from that tendon to the flexor surface of the radius, midway between elbow and carpus.

parts.name: Biceps profundus
parts.note: From the middle half of the posterior coracoid border, ventral to and partly overlapped by the superficialis and coracobrachialis brevis; a cord-like tendon along the ventral brachium to the bicipital tubercle of the ulna, partly uniting with the brachialis inferior.

occurrences.divisionNote: A double biceps characterises most turtles — Chelydra, other emydines, trionychids, Carettochelys and the pleurodires. **Testudo, Dermochelys and Lepidochelys have a single biceps**, and Walker (1947) showed from Chrysemys development that the complex begins as one mass and splits later, so the single condition is an unsplit one rather than a loss.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Crossing both shoulder and elbow, so a humeral retractor and an antebrachial flexor, the latter more important. Walker notes the insertion sits a long way from the elbow, which raises its mechanical advantage in flexion.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.note: = humeroantebrachialis sensu Diogo & Abdala (2007) and Diogo (2007); = short and long heads of biceps brachii sensu Jouffroy (1971).

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.note: Inferred from the biceps tubercle — an anteroposterior ridge on the lateroventral coracoid, named by Walker (1972) and treated as homologous across early crocodylomorphs by Crush (1980). Level I inference: the coracoid origin is bracketed by both Crocodylia and Aves.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete insertion tubercle on the radius.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: A very long tendon of origin from the ventral coracoid — about half the length of the belly — to the proximomedial radius.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A 6 mm tendon from the head of the coracoid, anchored to the ventral surface of the crista pectoralis by a tendinous band, running deep to the insertion of the pectoralis thoracicus. The tendon of insertion passes between the extensor metacarpi radialis and the brachialis to reach the tuberculum bicipitale on the caudal surface of the proximal radius, with a second branch on the tuberculum bicipitale of the ulna. Scored on the radial tuberosity because tuberculum bicipitale radii is the same site under another name. The biceps slip — a distinct avian belly running to the propatagial aponeurosis — is not scored: it ends in fascia.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii (long and short heads)
occurrences.action: Supinates the forearm and flexes the elbow.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The short head arises from the coracoid process — the fused remnant of the coracoid — rather than from a coracoid bone.

occurrences.name: Biceps longus + biceps brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus just caudal to the supracoracoideus from the ventral side of the procoracoid; brevis just caudal to the longus from the procoracoid and the adjacent lateral border of the stem of the interclavicle.
occurrences.insertion: Longus by a narrow aponeurosis on the radial edge of the ulna just distal to the brachialis ulnaris; brevis further distally by a wider aponeurosis on the radius, distal to and closer to the ulna than the brachialis radialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The origin is on the PROCORACOID and the interclavicle, bones no therian has — the therian biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and the coracoid process of the scapula. Allen (1912) denied any ulnar insertion of the biceps in this genus; Gambaryan et al. find one.
occurrences.divisionNote: Two heads, homologous with the therian caput longum and caput breve, but with the size relation reversed: the brevis is the larger in monotremes.

occurrences.name: Biceps longus + biceps brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus just caudal to the supracoracoideus from the ventral side of the procoracoid, penetrating under the lateral border of the stem of the interclavicle; brevis just caudal to it from the procoracoid and the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Longus by a narrow aponeurosis on the radial edge of the ulna just distal to the brachialis ulnaris; brevis by a wider aponeurosis on the radius, distal to the brachialis radialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The brevis is the only one of the two to reach the coracoid; both heads take the procoracoid.

occurrences.name: Biceps longus + biceps brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus just caudomedial to the supracoracoideus from the ventral side of the medial border of the procoracoid and a little from the dorsal side of the lateral border of the interclavicle stem; brevis further caudally from the ventral side of the caudal tip of the coracoid, just cranial to the coracobrachialis longus.
occurrences.insertion: The longus fuses with the brevis distal to the level of the pectoral crest and the two insert together on the posterior surface of the radius at its midlength, distal to the brachialis radialis, the longus' share of the common area remaining proximal to the brevis'.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The biceps longus has left the ulna: in both echidnas it inserts on the radial edge of the ulna and here it has moved onto the radius, fused with the brevis. A head changing which zeugopod bone it ends on, inside one clade.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.action: Flexes the antebrachium.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). The coracoid head is unequivocal, but **its site is fixed by negation**: the tendinous origin sits on a coracoid tubercle in crocodylians and birds, and early theropods such as *Coelophysis* and *Syntarsus* have no prominent or even distinct tubercle, so Burch places it anterior to the glenoid and just dorsal to the subglenoid fossa — where the tubercle would be. Supporting evidence comes from the coracohumeral/acrocoracohumeral ligament, which attaches very near this origin in both extant clades (Baier et al. 2007).

**The humeral head is scored disputed.** Only neognathous birds have one; in reptiles with two heads both arise from the coracoid. What supports it in *Tawa* is not the bracket but an oval striated depression on the anterior surface of the internal tuberosity, in the position the avian humeral head occupies. The ulnar insertion is likewise not crocodylian — crocodylians are usually described with a radial insertion only (though Reese 1915 reports a secondary ulnar attachment) — and comes from the lepidosaur outgroup, with a slight bulge on the anterior edge of *Tawa*'s ulna just distal to the articular surface as the correlate.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.action: Flexes the forearm and supinates it; the long head assists flexion of the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Long head from the supraglenoid tubercle, short head from the tip of the coracoid process, both to the radial tuberosity. **Both heads are coracoid heads in the outgroups** — in reptiles with two heads both arise from the coracoid, one tendinously and one fleshily, and only neognathous birds have evolved a humeral head. The human long head has migrated onto the scapula above the glenoid because the therian coracoid is reduced to a process of the scapula, so a change that looks like the muscle moving is the bone moving underneath it. Note also what is missing: the ulnar insertion present in lepidosaurs, reconstructed for *Tawa* and reported for some crocodylians is gone, leaving the radial tuberosity alone.

occurrences.name: M. biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). **Origin only, and the omission is the source's own.** Matsuoka & Hasegawa state that the insertion is surrounded by the proximal ulno-radial muscles and the attachment was not observed in this study, so no insertion row is written; leaving it empty reads as unrecorded, which is what it is. The main origin is a strong tendinous sheet from the craniolateral surface of the head of the coracoid, covering the Intumescentia on the cranial surface of the proximal humerus; the 'shoulder' of that tendon hooks onto the caudal surface and takes an accessory origin from the notch on the ventral slope of the Tuberculum ventrale. That second head is a humeral head — the state Burch (2014) notes is confined to neognathous birds among the taxa he surveyed, and which he scores as disputed for *Tawa* on the strength of a striated depression in the same position.

occurrences.name: M. biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Digastric, not two-headed** — a short muscular portion arising from the girdle over the secondary coracoid fenestra, then a tendinous band across the glenohumeral joint, then the main fleshy belly. The girdle origin is from the posteromedial border of the secondary coracoid fenestra and the medial coracoid plate nearby. Distally it unites with the brachialis anticus in a common pinnate insertion onto the proximal radius and ulna, described on that record. One head, from the coracoid, in the animal Burch uses as the lepidosaur outgroup for reconstructing the theropod biceps.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Two heads inserting together on the radial tuberosity. The distal head arises from the ventral surface of the coracoid, under the descendent part of the pectoralis, and its flat thin tendon runs over the coracobrachialis brevis; the proximal head is fusiform with parallel fibres and a stout tendon, lying laterally on the cranial face of the limb, and **arises from the humerus — the caudal surface of the deltopectoral crest — lateral to the tendon of the first head.** That humeral head is the disagreement with Russell & Bauer, who describe this animal's biceps as digastric rather than two-headed, arising only from the girdle at the posteromedial border of the secondary coracoid fenestra and inserting on the proximal radius and ulna together with the brachialis anticus. Freitas et al. state the point directly: in *V. exanthematicus* both heads arise from the coracoid, and in *Iguana* only the distal one does.

occurrences.name: M. coraco-antibrachialis (biceps brachii)
occurrences.innervation: N. coraco-brachialis proximally and N. musculo-cutaneus distally.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther called it the biceps brachii outright. Fleshy at both ends and tendinous in the middle — Osawa notes it becomes tendinous exactly at the shoulder joint and strongly fleshy again on the arm. From the medial border of the coracoid beside the supracoracoideus origin, to the proximal ends of radius and ulna and the elbow capsule. **Its two halves have different nerves**, the proximal from the N. coraco-brachialis and the distal from the musculocutaneous, which is the kind of split this dataset otherwise only records for the human flexor digitorum profundus.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Two tendons — one from the upper margin of the glenoid, one from the coracoid process — unite after a short course into a flattened tendinous band, and the belly is **undivided at first**, splitting only about the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the arm into a superficial coraco-radial part inserting on the radial tubercle and a deep gleno-ulnar part inserting with the brachialis anticus on the coronoid process of the ulna. So one of this muscle's two heads ends on the radius and the other on the ulna.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The same two insertions as the thylacine's, but **the bellies are distinct along their whole length** and only the tendons of origin partly fuse. Tear them apart upwards and the division shows: the gleno-ulnar part comes from the upper glenoid margin alone, while the coraco-radial part has both a coracoid and a glenoid origin — which makes that part alone, in this animal, the equivalent of the entire human biceps.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The same two insertions as the thylacine's, but **the bellies are distinct along their whole length** and only the tendons of origin partly fuse. Tear them apart upwards and the division shows: the gleno-ulnar part comes from the upper glenoid margin alone, while the coraco-radial part has both a coracoid and a glenoid origin — which makes that part alone, in this animal, the equivalent of the entire human biceps.

occurrences.name: Biceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. biceps.** A tendon 1.5 centimeters wide comes from the bicipital area of the ventro-anterior corner of the lateral face of the coracoid. This tendon always forms a part of the origin, but is not invariably used as MUSCLES OF THE WING a well for origin of M. tens. pat. longus and as insertion by part of M. pect., as indicated in figure 17. (See the descriptions of these muscles for other relationships).The larger head of origin of M. biceps is tendinous from the bicipital crest of the humerus; this head may receive twigs from N. brachialis longus superior. The two heads fuse completely one-third of the way distad on the humerus. Insertion—A ten *Insertion.* A tendon is formed about five-sixths of the way out the humerus; almost immediately it bifurcates to form two rounded tendons as it enters the antero-palmar part of the muscles of the forewing. En- trance is made just palmar to the entrance of N. brachialis longus superior and the superior brachial blood vessels. The two tendons are anconal to the insertion of M. brachialis. The insertion of the more anconal tendon is on the bicipital tubercle about one centimeter from the proximal end of the radius. Attachment by the other tendon is in the usual position on the ulna and some 2 centimeters from the proximal end of the olecranon process.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. biceps brachii.** Fig. 7 Muscle origins on the coracoid. A: Right coracoid in dorsal view, with osteological features labelled. B: Right coracoid in ventral view, with osteological features labelled. C: same as A, with muscle origin areas highlighted. D: same as B, with muscle origin areas highlighted. Scale bar = 20 mm. termuscular line separates it from the coracoidal origin of M. supracoracoideus. The insertion is by a diffuse tendon covering the apex of the ventral tubercle of the humerus, which leaves a large, ovoid impression with a rugose texture.

homology.notes: The coracoradialis/biceps field is continuous across Tetrapoda, distinguished from the brachialis by crossing the shoulder and inserting on the radius. Both are musculocutaneous-innervated, confirming shared ventral-mass derivation.

muscles.name: Coracobrachialis
synonyms: coracobrachialis superficialis/longus + profundus/brevis (Howell 1936a; Romer 1944; Jollie 1962; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Coracoid.
consensus.insertion: Medial or ventral surface of the humeral shaft.
consensus.action: Adducts and protracts (flexes) the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7) — ventral division.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain. Molnar et al. place the separation of the coracobrachialis from the pectoralis at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, marked by a distinct pectoralis process and coracobrachialis fossa on the humerus, and report no compelling evidence that it was a separate muscle in early tetrapodomorph fish.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Two small pits on the ventral scapulocoracoid between the anterior and posterior buttresses read as the origin, and a large, shallow recess on the proximal ventral humerus as the insertion (Andrews & Westoll 1970a). The humeral recess is one of two correlates identified in this taxon and in no other tetrapodomorph fish, which Molnar et al. flag as reason for caution; Gogonasus has a comparable knob-like process on the ventral side between the buttresses.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The rough, concave posterior region of the divided proximal ventral surface of the humerus (Coates 1996); the smooth anterior region beside it carries the supracoracoideus. Scored as humerus/ventral without a landmark — see the supracoracoideus row for why the anterior-posterior division between the two is in the note rather than in a second row.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Corresponds to the coracobrachialis longus/superficialis of Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its fibres run along the axis of the humerus to a distal insertion, so it retracts rather than adducts. Walthall & Ashley-Ross call it coracobrachialis longus; Abdala & Diogo record longus and superficialis as the same muscle.
occurrences.origin: Posterolateral surface of the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Medial face of the distal end of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis longus + brevis
occurrences.divisionNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Leiopelma clearly has BOTH coracobrachialis muscles, as described for Rana by Gaupp (1904), against Ritland's (1955b) account of Ascaphus. Sigurdsen et al. resolve the disagreement as nomenclatural rather than anatomical: Ritland's 'subcoracoscapularis' corresponds to the longus slip of the coracobrachialis. That is why this record's division and the subcoracoscapularis row have to be read together.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. From the coracoid to the medial face of the humerus. The coracobrachialis muscles of salamanders resemble those of frogs, so this is one of the conservative parts of the anuran forelimb.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis magnus + coracobrachialis brevis sensu Walker (1973) and Wyneken (2001).

parts.name: Coracobrachialis magnus
parts.note: Most of the dorsal coracoid onto the proximal border of the medial humeral process. Walker (1947) homologises it with the lizard coracobrachialis longus but renames it, since it does not reach as far distally.

parts.name: Coracobrachialis brevis
parts.note: Posterior border of the proximal half of the coracoid, into the intertubercular fossa. Homologous with the lizard coracobrachialis brevis.

occurrences.divisionNote: Walker separates two heads in *Pseudemys*. The extent of the brevis origin along the posterior coracoid border varies across turtles — the lateral half in *Testudo*, only the lateral fifth in *Emys*.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Rows are the union of the two heads; the parts say which is which. In *Pseudemys* many of the magnus's deeper fibres attach onto the subscapularis rather than to bone as they cross it, which is recorded here only in prose because a muscle is not a skeletal element.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis superficialis/longus + coracobrachialis profundus/brevis of earlier authors.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Inferred from a circular depression near the posterior margin of the lateroventral coracoid, shared with Dromicosuchus (NCSM 13733) and Terrestrisuchus. Crush (1980) read it as the attachment of the coracobrachialis anterior. Recorded here as an ORIGIN, which is this dataset's convention for the coracoid end; Crush and Bodenham et al. both word it as an insertion.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis brevis sensu Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Klinkhamer et al. divide this into brevis ventralis and brevis dorsalis. The ventralis is scored here — fleshy over the entire lateral coracoid to the deltopectoral crest. They give the dorsalis an anterolateral SCAPULAR origin, which is not a coracoid attachment and is not folded in.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis longus + brevis, or cranialis + caudalis, or anterior + posterior, depending on author.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar.

occurrences.name: M. coracobrachialis cranialis and caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Both parts, where this row previously held only the caudal one. Caudalis is one of two deep tongue-like muscles arising from the sternum, lateral to the supracoracoideus, from the craniolateral corner of the sternal plane and the ventrolateral surface of the base of the coracoid, inserting in the shallow notch on the dorsal slope of the Tuberculum ventrale. Cranialis arises from the dorsal slope of the head of the coracoid, immediately above the Impressio lig. acrocoracohumeralis, and inserts widely on the cranial surface of the proximal humerus — the area called Impressio m. coracobrachialis cranialis where the attachment is strong enough to leave a deep impression, **which Matsuoka & Hasegawa say it is not in this specimen**. A named osteological correlate recorded as not developed, which is the useful kind of negative observation for anyone reconstructing this muscle from a fossil.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin transfers to the coracoid process as the coracoid bone is lost.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis brevis + longus
occurrences.origin: Brevis from the ventral (external) side of the caudolateral border of the coracoid except its tip; longus from the ventral side of that tip.
occurrences.insertion: Brevis fleshy over the proximal ventral surface of the humerus from the crest of the lesser tubercle almost to the pectoral crest; longus in a sharply outlined triangular area on the ventral side of the postaxial border of the humerus, over its distal third up to the base of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The two are separated by a neurovascular bundle in Tachyglossidae, and the longus insertion leaves a defined facet on the bone in every genus.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis brevis + longus
occurrences.origin: Brevis from the ventral side of the caudolateral border of the coracoid just cranial to the longus and the subcoracoideus; longus by a tendon from the ventral side of the caudal tip of the coracoid, the tendon splitting into superficial, middle and deep aponeuroses.
occurrences.insertion: Brevis fleshy over the proximal ventral humerus from the crest of the lesser tubercle almost to the pectoral crest; longus in a distinct fossa on the ventral side of the postaxial border, over the distal half of the bone from the end of the pectoral crest to the base of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The longus fossa is a clean osteological correlate — a defined depression, not a roughened area.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis brevis + longus
occurrences.origin: Brevis from the ventral side of the caudolateral border of the coracoid except its tip AND from its dorsal (internal) surface up to the coracoid-procoracoid boundary, where it meets the subcoracoideus origin; longus by a narrow tendon from the ventral side of the caudal tip of the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Brevis over the whole proximal ventral surface of the humerus, but not adjoined distally by the longus; longus along a narrow line continuing the pectoral crest onto the ventral side of the base of the entepicondylus, at the level of the entepicondylar foramen.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The brevis has spread onto the internal face of the coracoid here, and its complete fusion with the subcoracoideus origin at the procoracoid boundary is what Gambaryan et al. take as evidence of the two muscles' close affinity — and what defeated Howell (1937), who lumped them as m. coracobrachialis profundus. The longus is crowded distally by the latissimus, which has shifted its insertion proximally onto the pectoral crest in this animal.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.action: Protracts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Both ends of the short coracobrachialis are unequivocal, and the long one is the weakest inference in the paper** — which is why this row is scored present and `single` rather than left uncertain. Origin from the posteroventral portion of the lateral coracoid, as in crocodylians and paleognaths and posterior to the biceps origin in neognaths; in many theropods the posteroventral coracoid process carries a distinct subglenoid fossa, which Jasinoski et al. (2006) identify as the site. Insertion on the anterior humerus distal to the proximal articular surface and onto the medial deltopectoral crest, where *Tawa* has a broad subtriangular depression with a distally pointing apex reaching just past the end of the crest.

**Coracobrachialis longus is deliberately not reconstructed, and the reason is not preservation.** Burch makes it a Level II' inference — his weakest category — because the muscle he would bracket it against is not homologous across the bracket: the Coracobrachialis longus of lepidosaurs belongs to the ventral mass with biceps and supracoracoideus, while the Coracobrachialis posterior of neognathous birds is a derivative of Subcoracoideus and part of the dorsal mass (Sullivan 1962; Romer 1944). He also regards it as simply absent in crocodyliforms: Jasinoski et al. (2006) reconstructed it as unequivocally present on Nicholls & Russell's (1985) report of it in crocodylians, but found it in none of their own dissections, and no other account of crocodylian musculature describes it. No amount of better material would settle a bracket that fails on homology. Langer et al. (2007) do reconstruct it; most workers follow Romer (1944) that its absence is plesiomorphic for archosaurs.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Coracoid process to the medial humerus at mid-shaft — a single belly where this record is a mass that carries two or three in the outgroups. The human muscle corresponds to the coracobrachialis medius; the brevis and longus of other tetrapods are not separately present. Its nerve is the reason it is worth reading beside the biceps and brachialis rows: all three are musculocutaneous, which is what identifies them as one ventral-mass series in the arm.

occurrences.name: M. coracobrachialis brevis and longus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Brevis is the anterior head, arising fleshily from the ventromedial coracoid behind the primary and secondary coracoid fenestrae, filling the area between the coracosternal articulation and the glenohumeral joint, and inserting on the posteroventral margin of the proximal humerus for about half its length. Longus lies deep to it, arises from the posterior coracoid process, and its belly twists and fans out to insert along the distal posteroventral humeral shaft between the brachialis anticus and the medial humeral head of triceps. **Both present and both coracoid** — which is the state Burch (2014) argues against for archosaurs, where he finds the longus absent in crocodyliforms and its homology with the neognath Coracobrachialis posterior broken.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Triangular, lying deep to the deltoideus clavicularis on the lateral margin of the pectoralis, from the cranial margin and ventral surface of the coracoid to a large stout tendon on the cranial edge of the deltopectoral crest and the medial face of the proximal humerus. Freitas et al. treat this muscle as anatomically conservative across reptiles and adopt the names Jenkins & Goslow (1983) and Romer (1944) use, which is why brevis and longus are separate entries in their tables where Russell & Bauer describe them as one two-part muscle. The insertion is the point of variation they draw out: on the deltopectoral crest here and in crocodilians and *V. exanthematicus*, but on the proximal humerus generally in the geckos and *L. agilis exigua*, and cranial to the crest in *Caiman latirostris*.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Fan-shaped, overlaid by the coracobrachialis brevis and the biceps brachii, with a belly of circular cross-section. Their table gives the origin simply as the coracoid; their discussion places it on the dorsal surface of the coracoid, alongside *L. agilis exigua* and the two geckos, so the row carries the dorsal side on the discussion's authority. It inserts on the middle third of the humerus, where Russell & Bauer trace the same muscle from the posterior coracoid process to the distal posteroventral shaft between the brachialis anticus and the medial triceps head. Freitas et al. contrast this with crocodilians, where the muscle arises from the scapula rather than the coracoid, and with *V. exanthematicus*, where it has two indistinct heads and reaches the epicondyle.

occurrences.name: M. coraco-brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *coraco-brachialis longus*, Günther's *coraco-brachialis inferior*. From the caudal angle of the coracoid, running obliquely to the medial anterior surface of the **distal third** of the humerus — a long muscle reaching almost to the elbow. **Osawa found it fused to the supracoracoideus in some specimens and cleanly separate in others**, with the N. coraco-brachialis passing between the two as the only reliable boundary; what Fürbringer called the coraco-brachialis brevis formed one continuous mass with the supracoracoideus, broken only by that nerve. A muscle boundary that exists as a nerve and not as a plane.

occurrences.name: Coraco-brachialis brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The short muscle alone**, which Cunningham notes is the carnivoran condition — a short thick fleshy muscle from the coracoid process in common with the coracoid head of the biceps, spreading fan-wise down over the subscapularis insertion to the humeral shaft immediately above the teres major. He is testing John Wood's account of the typical coraco-brachialis as a triple muscle, and these three marsupials give him brevis alone, brevis plus medius, and brevis plus longus in turn.

occurrences.name: Coraco-brachialis brevis and medius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The short muscle as in the thylacine, plus a **coraco-brachialis medius** — a very slender fasciculus inserted into the middle of the inner aspect of the humeral shaft.

occurrences.name: Coraco-brachialis brevis and longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The short muscle plus a **coraco-brachialis longus, inserted into the bridge of bone that walls in the supracondyloid foramen of the humerus** — the longest reach of this muscle in Cunningham's three animals, and an insertion that exists only because the foramen does. Cuvier & Laurillard figure both short and long slips in *Phalangista cavifrons*; Young found all three parts in the koala, with medius and longus fused.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. coracobrachialis anterior.** Fleshy and tendinous fibers arise from the antero-dorsal part of the coracoid; only tendinous origin comes from the tendon of origin of M. biceps, and the two tendons are inseparable ventrally. Insertion.—The insertion is superficially and anteriorly fleshy on the palmar surface of the humerus. The area extends distally as far as the distal end of the bicipital crest, but is delimited posteriorly by the bicipi- LIBRARY UNIVERSITY OF ILLeg 52 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE tal furrow and the proximal part of t *Insertion.* The insertion is superficially and anteriorly fleshy on the palmar surface of the humerus. The area extends distally as far as the distal end of the bicipital crest, but is delimited posteriorly by the bicipi- LIBRARY UNIVERSITY OF ILLeg 52 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE tal furrow and the proximal part of the base of the deltoid crest. Thus the insertion is deep to the insertion of the superficial part of the M. pect. and is bordered antero-proximally by the insertion of the fleshy anterior part of M. supracora

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis cranialis + caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. coracobrachialis cranialis.** This muscle is well-developed in Chauna. The origin is located on the dorsal head of the coracoid, covering the acrocoracohumeral ligament and extending onto a small strip of the coracoid itself. There is no osteological correlate of the origin of this muscle. The extensive fleshy insertion covers the coracobrachial impression on the proximal cranial humerus and extends onto the proximal half of the deltopectoral crest. Unusually among birds, the insertion leaves faint intermuscular lines on the deltopectoral crest, but the coracobrachial impression is not clearly defined. **M. coracobrachialis caudalis.** The origin of this muscle extends from the ventrolateral sternal end of the coracoid up onto the lateral coracoid shaft, in close association with M. subcoracoideus. homology.notes: Universal across Tetrapoda. Subdivision into two or three parts is frequent and independent; the number of parts carries no phylogenetic signal on its own. This muscle has the longest synonym list in the pectoral table — six naming schemes for the same field.
homology.teaching: Best illustration of why Abdala & Diogo's tables exist: the same muscle appears under six naming schemes across the literature.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

consensus.origin: Proximal humerus.
consensus.insertion: Radius.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow; in birds, tenses the propatagium — the leading-edge membrane of the wing.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]'.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete insertion tubercle on the radius, separate from the biceps one.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy from the deltopectoral crest, inserting with biceps and brachialis.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis / tensor propatagialis
occurrences.action: Tenses the propatagium, controlling the leading-edge camber of the wing.
occurrences.note: A striking case of exaptation: an archosaur elbow flexor recruited into the flight apparatus.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the antebrachium.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Neither correlate is in *Tawa*.** The origin is a rugose tuberosity distal to the deltopectoral crest on the lateral humeral shaft, which Jasinoski et al. (2006) found in maniraptorans and which matches the crocodylian scar; in basal taxa such a scar is rare, and the closest thing is a small rugosity anterior to the latissimus dorsi furrow in one specimen of *Herrerasaurus* (PVSJ 407). The insertion is a small tubercle on the anterior surface of the proximal radius, again seen in *Herrerasaurus* (PVSJ 373) rather than here. The reconstruction also carries the crocodylian ligamentous sling on the proximal radius that redirects the insertion tendon at the elbow (Meers 2003).

The homology is contested in both directions: sometimes a neomorphic archosaurian muscle (Meers 2003; Diogo & Abdala 2010), sometimes the homolog of the *Sphenodon* muscle of the same name (Romer 1944), whose dual innervation suggests a compound origin. Burch declines Meers's equation with the avian Propatagialis — those two share neither origin nor insertion — and assigns Propatagialis to the deltoideus clavicularis instead. Sullivan (1962) identified a distal part of the developing deltoid lobe in an early chicken embryo as a possible transitory vestige of this muscle, not retained in the adult.

occurrences.name: M. tensor propatagialis
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Arises from the dorsal surface at the base of the long apex of the furcula — the most anterior muscle attaching on the dorso-lateral surface of the clavicle-coracoid-scapula complex — with M. pectoralis pars propatagialis joining it from the proximal cranial surface of the Crista pectoralis. Its main tendon runs to the wrist like the bowstring of the arch the humerus and antebrachium form, with a weak tendon branching to the cranio-proximal ulna and radius, which is what the insertion rows record; the carpal ending is prose because it is a tendon into the propatagium rather than a bony attachment.

**Which record this belongs on is contested.** It is scored here because this record already carries tensor propatagii/tensor patagii as synonyms, following Meers (2003). Burch (2014) rejects that: he makes Propatagialis the homolog of the deltoideus clavicularis on Sullivan's and Howell's developmental evidence, and points out that the crocodylian humeroradialis and the avian propatagialis share neither origin nor insertion. The Tawa row on `deltoideus-clavicularis` states his side of it.

occurrences.note: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Absent, and the way it is absent is the interesting part.** Russell & Bauer state that the M. humeroradialis is absent in *Iguana* and in all other adult lizards, but does make a brief appearance during development. So the lepidosaur column on this record is a developmental presence and an adult absence — which bears directly on the contested homology of the crocodylian muscle, read by some as a neomorphic archosaurian muscle and by Romer (1944) as the homolog of the *Sphenodon* muscle of the same name. Sullivan (1962) likewise found a transitory vestige in a chicken embryo that the adult does not keep. Two clades in which the muscle exists only before hatching.

occurrences.name: M. humero-antibrachialis lateralis
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. **A weak muscle that barely reaches bone, and the reason it is scored here needs stating.** Osawa's muscle 21 — Günther's "the outer Muscle" — arises from the base of the processus lateralis humeri, from the end tendon of the scapulo-humeralis profundus and from the scapulohumeral ligament, and radiates into the radial antebrachial fascia, forming what Osawa calls a *lacertus fibrosus*. The insertion row on the radius stands for that fascial spread and is the weakest attachment in this column.

It is scored on this record because Romer (1944) homologised the crocodylian humeroradialis with the *Sphenodon* muscle of that name, which is one of the two live positions on this record — the other being that the crocodylian muscle is an archosaurian neomorph. Russell & Bauer report the muscle absent in *Iguana* and all adult lizards but present transiently in development, and that row is scored absent here. So the lepidosaur column now holds a tuatara that has something and lizards that do not, which is exactly the distribution the homology argument turns on.

homology.notes: An archosaur muscle on this sampling. The bird tensor propatagialis is the same muscle as the crocodylian humeroradialis; the many bird-specific names obscure a straightforward homology.
homology.teaching: The propatagial tensor is a genuinely good exaptation example, and one that students can see in any bird wing.
